summary.headline: Whether the flash size threshold has to hold under magnification, and whether user preferences or warnings can stand in for the requirement.

positions.label: Zoom must be accounted for
positions.detail: WCAG's philosophy is that criteria hold simultaneously, so a user who needs magnification must still be protected from seizure triggers; on a phone, 470 CSS px is most of the screen already. WilcoFiers proposes splitting the requirement in two — full-screen content such as video and games, where magnification is not expected, and everything else, where it is. mraccess77 adds that browser zoom is not assistive technology and that authors can read viewport scale.

positions.label: Zoom cannot be accounted for
positions.detail: GreggVan, who drove flashing into WCAG originally, states the intent was never that content be safe at arbitrary zoom — people with low vision also lean toward the screen, and no requirement can survive unbounded magnification. alastc's concern is false positives: failing content that harms nobody, which may be an acceptable trade against seizures but is the main cost.

positions.label: A warning is not a remedy
positions.detail: GreggVan's reductio — that WCAG could otherwise be replaced by a single site-wide "may not be safe for anyone with a disability" notice — went unrebutted on the substance. nattarnoff, who experiences these effects, says a warning makes them leave and look for an alternative rather than granting access. mraccess77 notes timestamps on a flashing video still do not deliver the missed information.

agreed: Warnings supplement the requirement; they do not satisfy it.
The flashing requirements and the separate flash-and-motion warning requirement have to be reconciled — #632 exists specifically to do that.
Some users deliberately want flashing — a Deaf user may want an audio alert mirrored visually — so a blanket prohibition is not the shape of the answer.
open: Whether the size threshold accounts for zoom, and whether to split full-screen from inline content.

Whether a user preference to prevent flashing can be relied on. alastc raised it and julierawe called relying on it dangerous; no accessibility-supported mechanism exists today, which the note in the draft currently presumes.
Whether responsibility for detecting and suppressing flashing sits with authors or with browsers — nattarnoff raised it, alastc noted the animation requirements have the same question.

threads.title: Pseudo-motion: Expand to include examples, and consider making this its own provision.

summary.headline: Whether the exception-free variant really is exception-free, given that a user preference or a disable mechanism could still be read as satisfying it, and whether pseudo-motion should be pulled out so no duration threshold can attach to it.

positions.label: The carve-outs are the whole problem
positions.detail: Opened #27 using WCAG 2.1 SC 2.3.3 as the cautionary example: it sits at AAA, it permits essential smooth animation, and it permits any smooth animation so long as some way to disable it exists, without requiring that the site-specific control be discoverable or that prefers-reduced-motion be honoured. Worries the essential exception will be stretched to cover any move or transition someone decided to make smooth. Notes many sites impose their own smooth scrolling regardless of prefers-reduced-motion or of browser settings to disable animation and autoplay, and that JavaScript-driven animation, including GitHub's own sticky headers, makes it harder still for users to protect themselves.

positions.label: Pseudo-motion should have no threshold and its own provision
positions.detail: The COGA Task Force filed #739 asking that pseudo-motion be defined with examples - parallax scrolling, sharp color changes, dynamically updating content, zoom effects, diagonal lines in a background, optical illusions, stereographic art - and that "No pseudo-motion" be split into its own provision, because the current wording can be misread as "does not include pseudo-motion lasting longer than 5 seconds", which is precisely the reading this no-exceptions variant is meant to foreclose. julierawe later added gamma oscillation images and sliced images. rachaelbradley offered the decoy font experiment as a candidate example and mraccess77 confirmed first-hand that those fonts appear blurry and give them a headache.

positions.label: A respected user preference is not a safe substitute
positions.detail: alastc opened #629 on the draft note allowing content to be considered as avoiding flashing when an accessibility-supported preference to prevent flashing is respected, doubting any such method is accessibility supported today and asking whether it should be relied on even if one were. julierawe, quoted in the body, calls the method dangerous and asks what happens when someone uses another person's device without having set the preference first. alastc flags in the body and again in June 2026 that the same question lands on the animation and reduced-motion requirements, which is how it reaches this provision.

positions.label: Warn first, or push detection down to the browser
positions.detail: patrickhlauke asks whether there should be a mandated warning before content containing potential flashing, with enough time for the user to abort or back out; alastc answers that a separate flash and motion warning requirement already exists in the working document. nattarnoff asks whether warning is an authoring duty at all or belongs to browsers detecting content type against the user's preferences, is unsure browsers could feasibly do it, but observes that we know what happens when it is left to the people who build sites, and argues this requirement straddles the bottom-up and audit-and-remediate approaches.

agreed: Pseudo-motion's definition needs worked examples; nobody objected to the COGA list or to the additions made to it.
The user-preference question is not confined to flashing - alastc stated twice that the animation-based requirements are impacted by it.
Warnings are already the subject of a separate requirement in the draft and are not what this provision does (alastc, #629).
open: Whether "no exceptions" also rules out satisfying the requirement via a disable mechanism or a user preference. MarjaE2 raised the mechanism form in #27 and it was never taken up; alastc's #629 raises the preference form and it is unresolved.
Whether "No pseudo-motion" becomes a provision in its own right (julierawe, #739).
Whether detecting motion and issuing warnings is an author responsibility or a user-agent one (nattarnoff, #629).
Whether the decoy font counts as pseudo-motion. rachaelbradley asked, mraccess77 gave a first-hand account of the effect, and no one has ruled on it.
summary.note: Thin, and largely inherited rather than specific to this variant. #27 is MarjaE2 alone - opened October 2023, one self-reply, no response from anyone else in nearly three years - and #629 and #739 are both labelled for the base No visual motion provision as well, so their discussion is shared. The only argument that bears directly on why an exception-free variant exists is julierawe's: that a five-second threshold sitting next to pseudo-motion reads as permission for anything shorter.

summary.headline: Whether honouring prefers-reduced-motion can satisfy the requirement, and whether motion harm belongs at the base level rather than as an optional extra.

positions.label: Not hurting users should be the floor
positions.detail: The WCAG 2 equivalent sits at AAA, which in practice means it is ignored. If a user has set prefers-reduced-motion, respecting it should be required, not aspirational. guyhickling argues a mechanism to stop animation is no help when the harm lands before the user reaches the control — particularly for keyboard users.

positions.label: "Reduced" is not "none"
positions.detail: prefers-reduced-motion is a single binary flag, but users are usually affected by specific kinds of motion, and the setting is sometimes enabled accidentally. Treating it as "turn off all animation" is too draconian for a normative requirement and risks developers writing WCAG off entirely.

positions.label: The group has stalled on measurement before
positions.detail: Defining size and duration across devices and zoom levels is where this previously broke down, and duration is undefined when the motion is triggered by user action such as scrolling. Moving it to a base level requires evidence of impact at a given size and speed, and a consensus process means persuading those who objected last time.

positions.label: The evidence cannot ethically be gathered
positions.detail: A study demonstrating harm from motion would harm its participants. Also argues the need is broader than vestibular illness: hyper-vigilance and attention impairments mean even small, sub-second animation costs time and mental energy to recover from.

agreed: "Pseudo-motion" needs examples in its definition. julierawe proposed parallax scrolling, sharp colour changes and dynamically updating content; rachaelbradley added decoy fonts and julierawe added gamma-oscillation and sliced images.
Real-world icon jiggle on hover and focus is a genuine problem, with mraccess77 supplying a live example.
Windows' reduced-motion setting is too coarse — mraccess77 reports it blocks animations they want along with those they do not.
open: Whether a user preference can be relied on to satisfy the requirement at all.

How to define a size and duration threshold that is testable without a screen ruler, which patrickhlauke raised as a reductio and mgifford answered by pointing out 4.5:1 looked equally arbitrary in 2008.
julierawe's separate objection (#733) that naming the guideline "Avoid Physical Harm" excludes the cognitive harm — lost focus, fatigue, re-orientation cost — that motion also causes.

summary.headline: Whether content-level properties that are not discrete triggers — the mood a piece of content creates, the storylines woven through it — can ever be pinned down well enough to be an outcome, or whether they belong to future assistive technology instead.

positions.label: Mood is a gap the current outcomes miss
positions.detail: Disturbing Content and Triggers only catch acute, identifiable items, but content can create a mood with nothing in it that flags as a trigger. SuzanneKTaylor's proposed outcome (#88) is that information about the mood content is likely to encourage is available or can be changed or selected by the user, aimed at long-form content — a movie, a television show, an ebook, a VR experience — where a user managing anxiety would benefit from knowing before committing. medeaoblongata frames the same gap as connotative content, distinct from denotative and from purely decorative, and notes that a detailed description can kill the effect it describes, since the sinister or the erotic is often about what goes unmentioned, so flagging a connotation in lieu of a description has value.

positions.label: Not measurable, and it adds noise
positions.detail: detlevhfischer's objection is that mood is not a property of content but depends on the user and on surrounding context, and that annotation would have to be exposed both visually and programmatically for equity, adding more material to the sea of content and increasing cognitive load for people it does not help — he does not see how this becomes a general measurable outcome. ericwbailey says it would be impossible to quantify before cultural variation is even factored in. patrickhlauke's concern is downstream: he dreads auditors having to check this kind of meta-information when judging conformance.

positions.label: Storyline selection as the tractable version
positions.detail: Issue #89 proposes that individual storylines be programmatically distinguishable, or that users can choose storylines. The argument is that hiding individual items leaves the surrounding context intact and so does not actually protect the user, while interwoven plots also tax memory and the ability to distinguish characters, locations and times. Her worked example is a video cutting between three people's stories in ten-minute and then five-minute blocks: being able to watch or skip one full story handles some subtle triggers by a simple mechanism rather than by content judgement.

positions.label: This is a job for AI-based AT
positions.detail: GreggVan argues no content can be written that triggers nobody — depending on personal history, a grove of trees could be a trigger — and that the group risks a never-ending discussion of what counts, so an AI filter that detects and redacts per the individual is the better place for it. SuzanneKTaylor partly agrees and extends it: if these outcomes live in AT, WCAG's remaining concern is whether that AT has the access it needs to pre-screen, which is a question about whether it can traverse a whole movie or gets stopped at the first ad. She adds that she personally thinks new AT is needed for many of the outcomes.

positions.label: Trigger profiles carry their own risk
positions.detail: The counter to GreggVan's AI filter is that the profile it needs is itself hazardous: asking a user to enumerate their triggers could be more triggering than the content, and a leaked profile could be used for serious harm — her example is a politician whose debate opponents obtain a copy. Her conclusion is that simple and common triggers, of the do-not-show-spiders-in-this-game kind, are addressable now, and outcomes may have to stay at that basic level until more is known.

agreed: If mood or connotation information exists, it should surface through a user agent, OS or screen reader setting the user has turned on, not by default. detlevhfischer conceded this removes the noise objection, while noting many users will never discover the setting.
There is a grey area between mood and content that some people treat as a trigger — detlevhfischer raised it and it went unchallenged.

Author-intended connotation is more tractable than user-experienced mood. SuzanneKTaylor concedes ericwbailey's point on her own proposal, since one reader finds a hardship story depressing and another finds it a call to action, and says that would need calibrating by the user inside AT.
open: Whether mood can be scoped into anything a conformance claim could be assessed against — detlevhfischer's question of where to stop is unanswered.
Whether AT could evaluate long-form content end to end, which is SuzanneKTaylor's own open question.
Whether storyline selection (#89) is worth pursuing at all. GreggVan's AI-filter response is the only substantive reply, and he was answering the trigger framing rather than the storyline mechanism.
summary.note: Both issues were filed by SuzanneKTaylor on the same day in 2024 in response to the May 2024 draft's call for missing outcomes, and both are thin. #89 has drawn two comments in over two years and no pushback on the storyline proposal itself; the discussion below is mostly #88, and the working group has not responded formally in either thread.

summary.headline: How far content warnings should reach beyond seizure and motion triggers into mood and mental health, and whether that is auditable at all.

positions.label: Add a mood outcome
positions.detail: Content can create a mood without containing any item identifiable as a trigger. Proposes that information about the mood content is likely to encourage be available or user-selectable, so that someone managing anxiety can decide before committing to long-form or XR content.

positions.label: There is a connotation gap
positions.detail: The current outcomes address denotative content and purely decorative content, but nothing addresses connotative aspects — what content implies or evokes as distinct from what it states.

positions.label: This is not auditable
positions.detail: Dreads a future where judging conformance requires auditors to check subjective mood metadata alongside everything else.

positions.label: Make it opt-in metadata, or leave it to AT
positions.detail: If mood annotations surface only through a user-agent or OS setting the user has turned on, they add no noise for anyone else. SuzanneKTaylor goes further: assistive technology may be the right place to pre-screen content, leaving WCAG responsible only for ensuring AT has the access it needs.

agreed: If such information exists it should be exposed on user request rather than presented to everyone by default.
open: Whether mood belongs in WCAG at all, or is properly an assistive-technology concern.
How to scope it so a conformance claim can be assessed.
How AT would evaluate long-form content — SuzanneKTaylor's own question is whether it could judge a whole film or would stop at the first scene.

summary.headline: Light discussion across two issues: a 2019-2020 exchange over whether disabled controls need a mandated icon or just adequate contrast, and a separate COGA request that explanations be persistent rather than transient.

positions.label: Require a disabled icon or 3:1 contrast
positions.detail: DavidMacDonald opened #197 noting that disabled interface elements work badly for people with low vision precisely because WCAG 2 exempts them from 1.4.3, and proposed requiring either 3:1 contrast or an icon marking the element as disabled. bkimmel seconds the problem, particularly where disabled states are used to signal future potential — fill these in and you can submit — calling the exemption a large safe harbour that cuts against the Perceivable goal. bkimmel is explicitly unsure an icon is the right remedy.

positions.label: Contrast yes, mandated icons no
positions.detail: Would rather see some minimum contrast applied to solve readability than have WCAG start demanding icons everywhere, which impinges on visual design decisions. Suggests a more general intent of "indicating that something is disabled" as the flexible form. Also notes a likely crossover with how user agents themselves indicate disabled state.

positions.label: The definitions do not cover disabled elements
positions.detail: Points out that "Interactive elements distinguishable" is adjacent to this problem, but the definition of interactive element — responds to user input and has a distinct programmatically determinable name — excludes disabled elements, which instead fall under non-interactive element. Since disabled elements are not mentioned in the examples or notes around that definition, he questions what the group actually intends, and floats broadening the term or adding a new one for elements that exist to be interactive but may conditionally be disabled or read-only. Flags this provision as also applicable and links w3c/wcag#5053.

positions.label: Explanations must persist long enough to read
positions.detail: Filing for the COGA Task Force in #783, notes the provision requires that information explaining why a control is disabled be available but says nothing about timing or persistence. A snackbar that vanishes after three seconds fails a user with slower processing speed. Recommends requiring explanations be persistent and visually co-located, and asks that this be checked for compatibility with "Notifications adjustable" in the User Control section. Cites MCU 3.1.2, 3.2.1, 3.7.5 and A.4.

agreed: Disabled controls being exempt from contrast requirements is a real low-vision problem worth addressing — nobody in #197 disputed the premise, only the remedy.
alastc took #197 off the WCAG 2.2 slate in 2020 as needing more work, consideration and research, and it has stayed there.
open: Whether the fix is contrast, an icon, or a technology-neutral requirement to indicate disabled state — patrickhlauke's objection to mandating icons has gone unanswered since 2020.
Whether the definitions of interactive and non-interactive element should be revised to account for disabled and read-only states, raised by adampage.
julierawe's persistence and co-location requirement, filed in August 2026 with no replies.
summary.note: #197 predates WCAG 3 and sat untouched from 2020 until adampage revived it in May 2026. #783 has drawn no response at all.

WCAG 3.0 Draft Guideline Captions

summary.headline: Whether WCAG 3 should prescribe how captions actually render, and whether closed captions should be preferred over open captions precisely because only closed captions can be adjusted.

positions.label: Captions need presentation standards, not just a requirement to exist
positions.detail: WCAG recommends captions but specifies nothing about whether the result is readable or usable. Proposes WCAG 3 adopt the Association of National Advertisers captioning standards, which are the basis for the FCC's television captioning rules and the National Park Service captioning guidelines. Filed as #119 in October 2024 and has drawn no reply from anyone in the thread.

positions.label: Closed captions should be rated above open captions
positions.detail: PoornimaSubramanian's case in #234 is user control: closed captions can be turned on and off, and can be customised for font face, size and position, so a rating should turn on the presence and accuracy of closed captioning, with a Rating 0 for informational or essential video carrying no metadata. WilcoFiers's opening question in #23 pushes further, asking whether open captions should be disallowed on new video material at all, and noting closed captions may be routable to a braille display. Neither has been answered in the threads.

positions.label: Open captions are not a conformance failure
positions.detail: Open captions are part of the time-based media, so they need no alternative text of their own; the alternative required at Level A is for the video. The video would fail 1.1.1 only if there were no text alternative identifying the video itself, and a transcript for audio information is not required until 1.2.8. Also corrects the video-only framing: captions are equivalents for audio, so video-only content has on-screen text, not captions.

positions.label: Open-captioned video should be required to carry a transcript
positions.detail: Opened by arguing open captions are literally images of text and so fail 1.4.5 at AA, or 1.1.1 at A if they lack alt text, since video frames have no alt text mechanism. Conceded awkawk's reading but held the underlying proposal: because captions are explicitly an alternative for audio, WCAG 3 should require open-captioned video to also have a text transcript. Raised as an edge case open-captioned instructional video whose only audio is royalty-free music, where the captioned information is effectively video-only time-based media.

positions.label: Do not carve out advertising or promotional video
positions.detail: mraccess77 argues exemptions are a regulator's job, since inaccessible video causes clear discrimination in areas such as fair housing and healthcare, and cites the shift on audio description for entertainment as precedent that entertainment is a right too. mitchellevan agrees on same weight, on the grounds that user needs and technical feasibility are the same, that "promotional" is hard to define, and that regulations such as the US Air Carrier Access Act already exempt advertising. Nobody argued the other side.

agreed: Open captions do not need their own alternative text, because they are part of the time-based media — awkawk's correction, which u9000-Nine accepted directly.
Whether advertising and promotional video is exempt is a matter for regulators rather than the technical standard; the point drew no rebuttal.

The reason to favour closed captions is adjustability — user control over display, font, size and position, and the possibility of routing to braille. Nobody argued the reverse case for open captions.
open: Whether open captions should be restricted or prohibited on new video material — WilcoFiers's question in #23, unanswered.
Whether WCAG 3 should import an external caption presentation standard — JLS2024's #119 is still without a single response.

How caption accuracy is graded. WilcoFiers asks how to weigh missing or wrong words, missing audio cues, missing speaker identification and missing punctuation needed to convey emphasis, sentence ends or sarcasm; no one has proposed a scheme.
Whether a rating keyed to the presence and accuracy of closed captions, as PoornimaSubramanian proposes, is workable as a conformance model.
u9000-Nine's edge case of open captions over a music-only audio track, which awkawk asked about and which was not resolved.

summary.headline: Three unconnected asks sit under this provision — fix WCAG 2's odd audio-only/audio+video split, tier caption quality alongside sign language, and merge the live caption requirements — and only the sign language one drew any reply.

positions.label: The WCAG 2 level split is backwards
positions.detail: Live audio+video requires captions at AA (SC 1.2.4) while live audio-only sits at AAA (SC 1.2.9), a split made when internet-radio-style audio streams were common and live video was technically onerous. Twitch, let's plays and live webinars have reversed that, and captioning either is equally hard. Taken to its conclusion, an author doing a live audio-only vlog is off the hook, but turning the camera on to show their face makes them fail. Raised in #189 in 2019 and carried forward with no reply on the substance.

positions.label: Tier caption quality, and name sign language explicitly
positions.detail: Auto-generated subtitles may be inaccurate and fail to carry tone and nuance, so captions alone do not deliver equitable access for Deaf people whose first language is signed (#325). Proposes graduated conformance: auto-generated or basic captions at Bronze, accurate descriptive captions plus context-appropriate sign language at Silver, and culturally appropriate sign language with multilingual caption options at Gold. Wants minimum quality guidance covering accuracy, speaker identification, emotional tone and cultural context.

positions.label: Levels are not settled, so level-based proposals are premature
positions.detail: Notes that Gold is likely achievable without doing everything listed at that level, and that the working group has not finalised what Bronze, Silver or Gold mean. Nothing definitive can be said about which tier anything lands in yet. Unrebutted, and the tiering discussion continued regardless.

positions.label: Merge the live caption requirements
positions.detail: Reads "Captions are available for all live audio content" as already covering several separate requirements about captions for live video, and suggests they be merged (#461). Filed as a short review note in December 2025 with no responses.

agreed: Auto-generated captions are not a substitute for accurate ones — nobody in #325 disputed the quality gap, only where it belongs in the conformance structure.
GreggVan's point that the conformance levels are unfinalised went unchallenged and constrains every level-specific proposal in #325.
open: Whether WCAG 3 keeps WCAG 2's distinction between live audio-only and live audio+video content at all — patrickhlauke's #189 is still open and unanswered after seven years.
Whether caption quality (accuracy, speaker identification, tone) becomes normative or stays as guidance — InfoGapBuster's proposal 5 in #325.
Whether the live captions requirement absorbs the separate live-video caption requirements, as MakotoUeki proposes in #461.

md84419 argues in #325 that the discussion is really about text alternatives and belongs in a new section under Text and Wording rather than Image and Media Alternatives, which would move it out of this provision's scope entirely.

summary.headline: Only one real argument happened here — whether open captions are images of text — and it was settled; the rest of the provision is unanswered proposals, including the request to define "important sounds", which drew no replies at all.

positions.label: Open captions are images of text
positions.detail: Argued in #23 that open captions are literally pixels of text burned into video frames, so they fail 1.4.5 Images of Text at AA, and fail 1.1.1 Non-text Content at A because no video frame carries alt text. Conceded awkawk's rebuttal on the alt-text point but held the substantive request: open-captioned video should be required to carry a textual transcript in WCAG 3, not only from 1.2.8 upward. Raised the edge case of instructional video with music-only audio, where the captions are effectively carrying video-only time-based media.

positions.label: Open captions already conform
positions.detail: Open captions are part of the time-based media, not separate non-text content, so the alternative required at Level A is the alternative for the video as a whole. Captions of either kind are equivalents for audio information, so the Prerecorded Video-Only provision u9000-Nine cited does not apply — video-only content has no audio and therefore no captions. Stated flatly that open captions pass Level A, full stop, and that a transcript for audio information is not required until 1.2.8.

positions.label: Speaker identification should be required
positions.detail: Argues in #23 that without knowing who said what, a story or issue becomes hard to follow, and that this is critical for people with face-blindness — Finnberrys identifies people by voice, so muted or inaccessible audio removes the only cue. Compares uncaptioned dialogue to reading a playscript with no character names, and cites Teams meetings, where visible names do the work that in-person recognition cannot. Makes the same case for blind users reading captions or a transcript on a braille display.

positions.label: Speaker identification is more contingent than that
positions.detail: u9000-Nine notes that identifying speakers by caption position on screen does nothing for someone with face-blindness, since the cue still depends on matching a location to a face. mitchellevan calls the discussion North-America-centric for assuming the identifier is text, pointing to the BBC's subtitle guidance recommending colour to distinguish speakers, a practice also common in continental Europe — while acknowledging colour identification may itself fail Use of Color. Neither rejects the need; both say the mechanism has not been pinned down.

positions.label: Exemptions belong to regulators, not the standard
positions.detail: On whether advertising and promotional video should carry less weight than primary content, mraccess77 points out that inaccessible video causes clear discrimination in areas such as fair housing and healthcare, and draws the parallel to audio description, once dismissed as unnecessary for entertainment until entertainment was recognised as a right too. mitchellevan agrees on equal weight: user needs and technical feasibility are the same, "promotional" resists definition, and regulations such as the US Air Carrier Access Act already carve out advertising where a jurisdiction wants that. Prioritisation should sit in regulation, not be baked into a technical standard.

positions.label: Captions alone do not give Deaf users access
positions.detail: InfoGapBuster, writing as a Deaf person in #325, argues auto-generated subtitles are inaccurate and lose tone and nuance, and that WCAG 2.0 putting sign language at AAA produced almost no implementation. Cites 250,000 to 500,000 primary ASL users in the US per Gallaudet, roughly 70 million Deaf people globally per the World Federation of the Deaf, about 60,000 JSL users in Japan, and 90 to 97 percent of Deaf children born to hearing parents with the resulting risk of language deprivation. Wants sign language translation — prepared in advance, distinct from live interpretation — named as a distinct outcome, arguing that requiring it would generate demand, grow the interpreter pool and accumulate training data. md84419 goes further, calling for a sign language alternative to website text and citing the BSL Act 2022, the Equality Act 2010, the Irish Sign Language Act 2017, the Korean Sign Language Act 2016 and the New Zealand Sign Language Act 2006 as evidence that language-based discrimination is already legally constrained.

agreed: Advertising and promotional video should carry the same weight as primary content in the standard itself, with any exemption left to regulators — mraccess77 and mitchellevan, unrebutted.

awkawk's reading that open captions are part of the time-based media and need no alternative text of their own was accepted by u9000-Nine ("That is fair"), narrowing the dispute to whether a transcript should also be required.
GreggVan's procedural point that no conformance level has been finalised, so nothing definitive can be said about what Bronze, Silver or Gold require, went unchallenged.
open: What counts as an "important sound". sydneycolemanfromgoogle opened #525 arguing the term is subjective and leads to missing context; the issue has no replies.
Whether open-captioned video must also provide a textual transcript in WCAG 3 — u9000-Nine's core request in #23, which awkawk acknowledged as clear but did not agree or disagree with.
Whether speaker identification is required, and whether text, colour or caption position satisfies it — raised by Finnberrys, complicated by u9000-Nine and mitchellevan.

Whether closed captions should be preferred over open captions, or open captions barred on new material, and how caption accuracy is graded across missing words, missing audio cues, absent speaker labels and punctuation carrying emphasis or sarcasm — all posed in WilcoFiers's original #23 body and none answered.
Whether MakotoUeki's proposal in #463 to merge other prerecorded-caption requirements into this one is accepted; the issue has drawn no comments since December 2025.

Whether the sign-language material belongs under this provision at all. md84419 argues in #325 that what is being discussed is text alternatives and needs a new section in 2.2 Text and Wording rather than 2.1 Image and Media Alternatives.

summary.headline: Whether speaker identification in captions should be required at all, and whether naming the speaker in text is the mechanism or just a North-American assumption.

positions.label: Required wherever the speaker can be identified
positions.detail: Understanding a conversation often depends on who said what, and without the who a story or issue becomes hard to follow — like reading a playscript with no characters identified. Speaks from experience of face-blindness: usually identifies people by voice, so on a muted device or with a hearing impairment, following a conversation between people who look similar is very difficult. Compares captions carrying names to a Teams meeting, where every participant's name is visible, versus an in-person one. Extends the same argument to blind users reading captions or a transcript via braille.

positions.label: Positional identification does not do the job
positions.detail: Identifying a speaker by where the caption is placed on screen does not help someone with face-blindness. Narrow but unrebutted; Finnberrys's reply effectively concedes it by restating that what helps is a name in the caption, not a position.

positions.label: Text is not the only convention
positions.detail: The discussion is North-America-centric in assuming the identifier is text. The BBC recommends colours to distinguish speakers, and the practice is common in continental Europe. Explicitly does not claim colour is better than text, or even that it is accessible — flags that it might fail Use of Color — but argues the provision needs international context before it settles on a mechanism.

positions.label: Scope is wrong for speakers who are not systematically identifiable
positions.detail: In #512: in a live meeting or its recording, several people sharing a room are grouped as a room rather than identified individually, so the provision should say it is limited to speakers who are systematically identifiable. Second case is a video with one speaker who introduces themselves at the start, where announcing the speaker every time is repetitive. Concludes the provision needs more work or should remain supplemental for now.

positions.label: Applicability is drawn too narrowly
positions.detail: In #748: the provision applies only when there are multiple speakers in the video, which should be generalised to media so it covers audio without video, video without audio, and video with audio.

positions.label: The notes need worked examples
positions.detail: In #472: each note under the foundational wording — full name then part of name, hidden identity as part of narrative structure, recognisable position within the context of use — needs a concrete example. The only example the provision carries is the Maya Angelou to Angelou shortening.

agreed: The user need reaches beyond deafness — face-blindness, braille readers and muted-device situations all appear in Finnberrys's case and nobody disputed any of them.
Nothing distinguishes the captions version of this provision from the transcripts or audio-description versions; all four threads are labelled across all three at once.
open: Whether speaker identification is required at all. WilcoFiers's opening question in #23 asks exactly this and Finnberrys is the only person who answered it directly.
Whether colour or caption position count as identification, and how that squares with Use of Color — mitchellevan raised it and it has not been taken up.
Whether the provision should be limited to systematically identifiable speakers, and how to handle a single self-introducing speaker — sydneycolemanfromgoogle, #512.
Whether "video" becomes "media" in the applies-when clause — ashleemboyer, #748.
How missing speaker identification would be weighted in any caption accuracy grading — one strand of WilcoFiers's accuracy question in #23, covered under Captions adjustable.

summary.headline: Whether WCAG 3's "decorative" has quietly widened WCAG 2's "pure decoration" into a loophole, and whether the fix is a tighter definition, a second tier of decorative images that may carry alt text, or abolishing the exemption entirely.

positions.label: Abolish the exemption
positions.detail: ericwbailey's framing in #238 is that an abled content author deciding what counts as decorative removes agency from the person using assistive technology, and he supplies a case he met in the wild: photos of amenities for luxury housing classed as decorative even though they communicate the benefit of living there. brett-oppegaard escalates this in #369 — a designer told him a stock photo of a diverse group reading books in front of a university building was decorative and therefore not legally required to be described, and he has heard the same claim made about portrait photos of organizational leaders. His argument is that visual designers always have the option not to include an image, so every included image has a rhetorical purpose; that a screen reader user can skip alt text with a single keypress, so the audience should decide, not millions of decentralized, busy, often untrained site managers; and that the loophole is why Instagram alone emits 70,000 mostly undescribed images a minute. He also wants the term "alt text" retired in favour of static Audio Description, which he argues separately in #371 (see image-alternatives-available).

positions.label: Over-description is its own barrier
positions.detail: TestPartners reports content creators over-compensating with literal descriptions of decorative images running to several sentences and as much as 50 words, which a screen reader user must sit through a large proportion of before concluding it is fluff they did not need; he puts community opinion at roughly 50:50 and says a substantial majority should exist before anything changes. He half-seriously proposed a CSS prefers-reduced-fluff property as the only way to satisfy both camps, and rejects the premise that undescribed decorative images discriminate — you may as well argue that hanging wallpaper discriminates against people who cannot see it. patrickhlauke's reductio in #238 is that if every non-text piece of information must be conveyed, authors would have to describe colour and sizing choices and ultimately the entire CSS of the page, so a pragmatic and admittedly subjective cut-off is unavoidable; he adds that where a flourish exists to convey a mood, prose carrying the same tone can already be an acceptable alternative. bruce-usab makes the placement argument against Myndex's paisley example: the fact that paisley patterns descend from Jacquard-loom punch cards is compelling trivia that belongs in the footer or on an About page available to everyone, not buried in an alt attribute forced only on screen reader users.

positions.label: Hold the WCAG 2 line
positions.detail: yatil's objection in #369 is that WCAG has said "pure decoration" since 2008 and merely being decorative never qualified for the exception — WCAG comes from the era of image-rendered container shadows and image-replacement headings, and most genuinely pure decoration can now be done in CSS. He argues the draft's test, whether removing the image would impact how people understand the page, is far too low a bar: under it a portrait in a staff index is decorative and so is a news article photo, and neither "impact" nor "understand" is defined. lauracarlson opened #238 on the narrower charge that "Decorative Images" is broader than "Pure Decoration" and that conflating them is a mistake; her specific target is the Method's "Illustrative of adjacent text but not contributing information (eye-candy)" line, and she proposed renaming "Decorative" to "Purely Decorative" throughout. Both she and bruce-usab call null alt overused and a hangover from the spacer-gif era, though bruce-usab says his own sampling shows missing alt and low-information alt attempted as textual equivalence remain the bigger problems.

positions.label: Two tiers, with alt optional on the softer one
positions.detail: MakotoUeki opened #466 proposing an explicit split: purely decorative images (an icon alongside text, a thumbnail inside a link) need no text alternative and should have no accessible name, while decorative images (a photo, an illustration) may usefully carry one as a best practice. The user need he cites is a person who lost their sight later in life and wants the description in order to picture the image, and his position in #238 is that the user, not the author, should decide whether something is meaningless. fstrr points at a ready-made middle category: the HTML spec's ancillary images, where an image is neither purely decorative nor entirely redundant with the text, the alt attribute must be present, its value may be the empty string or a textual representation, and it must not be empty when the image has a caption.

positions.label: One category, defined properly
positions.detail: grace-snow's reply in #466 is that if an image adds meaning it is not decorative at all, so naming a class of "decorative" images that do need alternative text is highly likely to confuse; whether a photo or illustration is decorative depends on the surrounding content and context, not on the image type. Finnberrys agrees and offers the substitution test she applies: a swirly line at the bottom of a page could be swapped for a wiggly rainbow line with no effect on content, whereas a photo of her dog on a page about assistance dogs could not be swapped for a unicorn without becoming confusing and weird. sydneycolemanfromgoogle filed the same objection independently in #518 — the distinction is not useful without a clear and mostly objective means of telling the two apart.

positions.label: The gap is in user agents, not author judgement
positions.detail: mraccess77 reports that Internet Explorer's exposure of alt as a tooltip let him learn things about images he could not distinguish visually — essentially audio description for the web, the nuances low-vision users miss — and notes that captions today are available to everyone rather than only to deaf users, while accessible name and description are not. Myndex makes the adoption argument: alt text is effectively unreachable outside screen reader use, and if it surfaced through a standard user-agent affordance it would serve people with prosopagnosia or other cognitive and contextual needs, reader mode, and failed image loads, and the broader demand would drive adoption. bruce-usab counters from history that IE's tooltip behaviour is precisely what trained authors to write tooltips into alt for years, that the TITLE attribute only partly separated them, and that the practice only corrected when touch UIs removed the tooltip. Myndex also flags that CSS background images accept no alt text at all, which he treats as a missing platform property rather than an author failing.

agreed: Null alt is overused and "decorative" gets stretched to cover images that inform — bruce-usab and MakotoUeki both concede this to lauracarlson, and no one in nine threads defends the current breadth.
yatil's asymmetry argument went unrebutted: information that is present can be skipped by the user, information that was never provided cannot be recovered.

Applying the exemption is a judgement call with no single right answer. jake-abma's evidence is the WCAG 2.1 CSS-fitting-images working example, which shipped with alt="" and which mraccess77 said during sanity-checking he would rather have had described.

The drafted test procedure is defective and nobody has argued otherwise. grace-snow (#573) shows it is written only for img, ignores svg and role="img", omits that role="img" must be absent from a decorative image, and omits aria-hidden="true" as a technique; JasonAment (#607) shows the first procedure's help text duplicates a condition of the second; janBeniaminKwiek (#614) asks that "add no information to the content" become "add no information or functionality".

The self-contradiction WilcoFiers raises in #495 is unanswered: if content is what is communicated to the user and a decorative image is by definition not that, then a decorative image cannot have programmatically determinable properties and therefore cannot be programmatically hidden. He recommends reverting to WCAG 2.0's definition of programmatically determined, which lacks the word "important".

The overlap with Images detectable that scottaohara raised via #357 — how can an image be hidden and detectable at once, and where do CSS background images land — was resolved editorially; scottaohara accepted the reworked text in the Jan 5 draft preview and adampage closed the issue on 2026-04-01.
open: Whether "decorative" should be one category or two. MakotoUeki (#466) wants the split; grace-snow, Finnberrys and sydneycolemanfromgoogle want one term defined well. adampage closed sydneycolemanfromgoogle's #518 as a duplicate of #466 rather than answering it, so the question sits entirely in #466.

Whether the exemption should exist at all. brett-oppegaard's #369 poses it as five direct questions — what the exemption is for, who it serves, what the downside of removing it is, whether the old page-weight rationale still applies, and whether WCAG is obliged to define "decorative" in a legal sense — and none has been answered on the record.
Whether the author or the user decides an image is meaningless. ericwbailey, MakotoUeki and jake-abma all land on the user; nobody has proposed a mechanism that would let them.

What research supports widening "pure decoration" to "decorative". lauracarlson asked for the data in January 2022 and again in her follow-up; jake-abma's answer was that data is not always available and the judgement is inherently subjective. No study has been cited in either direction.
Whether CSS background images can carry alternatives at all — Myndex raised it in #238 and it is the same hole scottaohara found from the Images detectable side in #357.

Whether authors should be describing emotionally rich images and, if so, how. lauracarlson pointed at Léonie Watson's and Jake Archibald's writing on emotion in text descriptions; the thread did not take it up.
WilcoFiers' definitional contradiction (#495) and grace-snow's test rewrite (#573) both need an editorial decision; neither has drawn a single reply.
summary.note: This provision's history runs in two disconnected halves. #238 was argued out in January 2022, bruce-usab took the concrete fix to EOWG as a pull request against the WAI tutorial (wai-tutorials#635), it was considered and declined, and he asked lauracarlson to close; she declined in September 2022 on the grounds that the full AG Working Group should consider it and that WCAG 3 should not inherit the tutorial's examples. The issue then sat untouched for three years until brett-oppegaard revived the argument in September 2025. Several of the more consequential recent filings — #495, #573, #607, #614 — are single unanswered comments, so the quality of the current draft text has had far less scrutiny than the definition has. Note also that brett-oppegaard participates by email, so his comments arrive with quoted reply chains attached.

summary.headline: Whether "available" means available to everyone or only through assistive technology, and whether "equivalent" is a definition problem the standard can fix or a practice problem it cannot.

positions.label: Available should mean visible, not just programmatic
positions.detail: MarcHaunschild opened #191 arguing there is no icon everyone understands, and that an aria-label serves only screen reader users — the sighted majority, people who do not read the Latin alphabet, and speech-input users get nothing. His example is the GitHub editor toolbar, where a large A beside a small A could equally mean resize text; it actually means add header text, and he says he would never have guessed. He reports Germany's BITV-Test once required textual descriptions for icons and dropped the requirement to align with WCAG, which he treats as a regression. alastc drafted the requirement as "a visible text equivalent for icons is available" with icon defined as a non-text representation of a function or discrete piece of information, such as a printer for print or a green tick for complete; MarcHaunschild accepted it and asked for an "unless essential" carve-out for cases such as a game where guessing the shape is the point.

positions.label: It was tried and no mechanism survived touch
positions.detail: alastc reported in March 2020 that DavidMacDonald's proposal was worked through in the group and put to a member survey, and that coverage broke down across four scenarios: active and inactive icons, on mouse and on touchscreen. A hover tooltip handles the mouse cases cleanly, but on a touchscreen the user cannot reach the text without activating the control or relying on a flaky double tap, and forcing visible labels into a toolbar destroys the toolbar's purpose. LJWatson cautioned separately against title attributes and the SVG title element becoming the recommended route, since those tooltips are not dismissable; awkawk noted 1.4.13's exception for user-agent-controlled presentation makes them technically permissible, and LJWatson accepted the exemption while maintaining the practice should not be encouraged. detlevhfischer pushed back on the related proposal to extend Label in Name to graphical buttons, asking what a speech-input user would actually say — "click i", "click italics" — and pointing to the existing symbolic-text-characters exception as the right answer.

positions.label: Equivalence has collapsed into a compliance formality
positions.detail: His #370 argument is that "equivalent" has been so weakly defined that a file name passes in practice: "dog32234.jpg" tells you nothing about breed, setting, activity or the rhetorical reason the image was chosen, and he demonstrates the gap by asking whether readers pictured a French Bulldog on a Hawaiian beach or a Rottweiler on a grassy field. He cites Perkins at under 1 percent of the web compliant, AudioEye at roughly 3 percent and WebAIM at 4 percent, and argues Instagram's billion-plus uploads a day are being pushed toward GenAI descriptions of the form "Might be a man, wearing glasses". He wants equivalence defined against the academic literature on information exchange and extended explicitly to maps, charts, tables, data visualizations and descriptions of people, rather than a title plus a one-sentence overview. In #371 he makes the parallel terminology case: "image" excludes maps, charts and data visualizations in most people's minds, and WCAG should adopt static Audio Description, the term used by the American Council of the Blind, the American Foundation for the Blind, RNIB, the World Blind Union, the American Alliance of Museums and the US National Park Service, over image description, which is largely a computer-science coinage.

positions.label: The requirement is sound; the ecosystem is not
positions.detail: patrickhlauke's first reply is a flat correction: "dog32234.jpg" does not pass, it fails 1.1.1 as an inappropriate text alternative. TestPartners argues authors misusing text alternatives is not a loophole — testers frequently do not test the criterion correctly, automated tools cannot yet judge appropriateness, and the root causes are education and authoring platforms that do not help; WCAG 3 cannot and will not fix that. He adds a newer structural cause: organizations now store images in digital asset management systems with the alt text attached, so the text is written with no knowledge of the context it will be used in, which is why it defaults to a literal description of the image contents. yatil makes the division-of-labour point — W3C defines conformance, laws enforce it, and under the European Accessibility Act member states must stand up agencies with fines behind EN 301 549's reference to WCAG 2.1.

positions.label: Equivalence is the wrong goal to aim at
positions.detail: In #272 he asks the group to revisit his proposal "Meaningful images have a text alternative" in place of the current goal that users have equivalent alternatives. His grounds are that decades of evidence show equivalence at scale does not work — he cites WebAIM's finding that nearly a third of images on popular home pages have missing, questionable or repetitive alternative text — and that even where alt text exists there is no agreement on what an equivalent is: ask ten experts and you get ten answers, with far wider spread in the wild. He frames the fix as inter-rater reliability, pointing to slides he presented to the working group three years earlier, and argues a meaningfulness test is both more scalable now and better positioned for changes in technology.

positions.label: Equivalent to what, exactly
positions.detail: #499 takes the draft sentence on its own terms: "Equivalent text alternatives are available for images that convey content" does not say what the alternative must be equivalent to. He notes that someone carrying WCAG 2 knowledge assumes the intent is the purpose of the image, but read cold the wording points at the content of the image instead — under which "House icon" would be correct and "home" would not.

agreed: The state of alt text in the wild is poor. brett-oppegaard, mbgower and TestPartners cite overlapping evidence for it and disagree only about whether the standard is implicated in the cause.

patrickhlauke's correction that a file-name alt already fails WCAG 2.x 1.1.1 was not contested on the merits; brett-oppegaard moved to enforcement and interpretation rather than defending the original claim.

yatil's account of where the buck stops — W3C sets the standard, civil rights law and the EAA enforce it, and W3C has neither budget nor intent to review billions of sites — was accepted by brett-oppegaard, who redirected to the DOJ Title II rule.

TestPartners' digital-asset-management argument is unrebutted and brett-oppegaard endorsed the underlying problem, agreeing descriptions should be crafted per use and logged so a recontextualization trail exists, while conceding that would require a major shift in archiving practice.
Nobody defended the title attribute or the SVG title element as the technique to recommend, even after awkawk established it is permissible under 1.4.13's user-agent exception.

alastc's 2020 finding that no icon-text mechanism worked as a potentially legal requirement across sites and devices stands unrebutted; his suggestion that the work survive as advisory techniques drew no reply.
open: Whether a visible text equivalent for icons should be required at all. MarcHaunschild's #191 has had no substantive comment since alastc reported the survey outcome in March 2020, and no one has proposed a touchscreen mechanism since.
Whether "equivalent" is measured against the image's content or its purpose. WilcoFiers raised it in #499 in January 2026 and the issue has no replies.

Whether the provision must say something specific about maps, charts, tables and data visualizations rather than treating them as images. brett-oppegaard asked for it in #370 and it was not taken up in a thread that turned to enforcement instead.

Whether "image" and "alt text" should be retired in favour of static Audio Description. brett-oppegaard's #371 has been open since September 2025 with zero comments, so the terminology argument the decorative-images threads defer to here has in fact never been answered.
Whether mbgower's meaningfulness framing replaces the equivalence goal. He asked twice in July 2025 and offered to walk the group through it; no one has responded on the issue.

Whether WCAG should say anything about over-specifying attributes in a description. rusteinberg's #251 raises the risk of an author writing "African American man working on his computer" about someone who is neither, and suggests "Man working on his computer" instead; MakotoUeki, then the Alt Text subgroup lead, asked which writing guide the advice came from in November 2021 and the thread stopped there.

MarcHaunschild's "unless it is essential to be without text" exception, and detlevhfischer's question of what a speech-input user would say for a graphical button, were both raised once and never examined.
summary.note: This provision is discussed far less than its filing count suggests: 7 threads and 23 comments, of which #370 accounts for most of the exchange and three others (#251, #371, #499) are effectively unanswered. #191 predates WCAG 3's provision structure by six years, and the substantive record for it — the acceptance survey alastc worked from — sits behind a W3C member-only link, so the reasoning for dropping the icon requirement is not publicly readable here. sydneycolemanfromgoogle's #518, on the decorative versus purely decorative distinction, is labelled against this provision but adampage closed it as a duplicate of #466, which moves that whole argument into the decorative-images-hidden record. As there, brett-oppegaard participates by email, so his comments arrive with quoted reply chains attached.

summary.headline: Whether "equivalent" is failing because the definition is too loose or because the existing requirement is simply not being tested and enforced properly.

positions.label: Define equivalence, or the gap stays open
positions.detail: In #370, argues alt text is a legacy of early image-loading problems rather than a disability-studies concept, and that in practice a filename like "dog32234.jpg" is treated as compliance. Cites Perkins at under 1 percent of the web compliant, AudioEye at around 3 percent and WebAIM's Million at 4 percent to argue the failure is systemic rather than incidental. Wants "equivalent" defined against the information-exchange literature and extended with guidance for describing people, maps, tables, charts and data visualisations, not just a title plus a one-sentence overview. Points at Instagram, where alt text is buried behind a hidden process and GenAI supplies descriptions like "Might be a man, wearing glasses".

positions.label: That already fails WCAG 2 — this is not a loophole
positions.detail: patrickhlauke's opening reply is flat: "dog32234.jpg" would fail 1.1.1, so it is not legally compliant in any sense. TestPartners attributes the observed state to testers not testing the criterion correctly, automated tools being unable to judge appropriateness, and authoring platforms that do not help — a lack of education, not a defect in the wording, and something WCAG 3 cannot fix. yatil adds the structural point that W3C defines conformance and does not enforce it; enforcement runs through civil rights litigation and, in the EU, through the European Accessibility Act's reference to WCAG 2.1 via EN 301 549, with national agencies and fines that only began operating this year.

positions.label: Digital asset management is making it worse
positions.detail: TestPartners identifies a newer failure mode: organisations now store images in a DAM with the text alternative attached to the asset, so the alternative is authored with no knowledge of the context it will appear in, and ends up an invariably literal description of image contents that may be appropriate in one placement and wrong in another. brett-oppegaard accepts the point, proposes that descriptions be crafted per use and logged so a forensic recontextualisation is possible, and concedes this would require a major shift in archiving practice. Both treat it as a real problem; neither claims it is the central one.

positions.label: Media alternatives are undertested as a single lump
positions.detail: In #611, argues the draft never says which formats are usable for which medium and that the media alternative definition adds nothing. Offers an absurd-but-passing case: video-only content with an empty closed caption track satisfies the requirement as written. Proposes splitting the test procedure into separate procedures for audio-only, video-only and audio-video content, each ending in a check that the alternative is equivalent to the meaningful information in the media.

agreed: "dog32234.jpg" is not conformant under WCAG 2.x 1.1.1 — brett-oppegaard did not contest patrickhlauke's correction, and shifted to arguing about enforcement instead.
Real-world conformance rates are very low; the disagreement is about the cause, not the number.
W3C neither polices nor funds review of conformance claims; that sits with law, regulators and litigation.
open: Whether WCAG 3 should tighten the definition of equivalent and add scaffolding, metrics and benchmarks — brett-oppegaard's core ask, which nobody in the thread endorsed or costed.

What recourse exists against a false "this website is WCAG compliant" claim, and how many violations would invalidate it. brett-oppegaard asked directly; yatil answered only on the general enforcement landscape.
Whether equivalence guidance should extend to specific content types — described people, maps, charts, data visualisations — beyond generic image alternatives.
JasonAment's proposed per-medium test procedures in #611.
summary.note: Thin and lopsided. #370 is essentially brett-oppegaard against three respondents who all make the same rebuttal, and the exchange drifts from defining equivalence into enforcement and legal policy without returning. #611 is a body with a concrete proposal and zero replies, so nothing there has been tested at all.

summary.headline: Nobody can say what "detectable" means — the disagreement is whether it needs a normative definition or whether the requirement should be dropped as redundant.

positions.label: Drop it — it does not make sense
positions.detail: Calls "Non-decorative images are detectable" painfully vague and asks the specific questions the text cannot answer: detectable to whom, what counts as detectable, whether sighted users need to know an image of text is an image, and whether the obligation is programmatic and if so over which part — role, accessible name, or both (#494). Observes that role and name already appear to be covered by other requirements, so if that is not what this means, nothing is left. Recommendation is to remove the requirement.

positions.label: Keep it, but define it normatively
positions.detail: Agrees the term is ambiguous but proposes a fix rather than deletion (#605): "A detectable element is one that can be identified programmatically in code and is presented to users in a way they can perceive." Points out that the only place the concept is currently explained is the non-normative Test section, which is not a basis for consistent interpretation or enforcement.

positions.label: The test conflates two modalities
positions.detail: Folding code inspection and screen reader inspection into one test case invites incorrect interpretation; JasonAment proposes splitting them into parallel tests with alternate conditions — check the markup where a code inspector can reach the image, and use a screen reader only where the code cannot be checked (#606). mraccess77 adds that the accessibility API should be checked before jumping to a screen reader test.

positions.label: The requirement collides with decorative images
positions.detail: Raised as a review comment on PR 350 and carried into #357: does this forbid CSS background images unless they are also marked up as images, and how does it square with the decorative-image requirement that such images be programmatically hidden? If an image is hidden it cannot be determinable as an image, which suggests the requirement is really about images that convey meaning. scottaohara later confirmed the draft preview updates to both requirements addressed this, and adampage closed the issue on 2026-04-01 after verifying the editor's draft.

positions.label: Markup presence is not the test
positions.detail: MakotoUeki asks whether "non-decorative images" can simply be defined as "images that convey meaning", and whether in HTML using an img element satisfies the requirement (#467). mraccess77 answers no: use of img does not by itself mean the image is anything other than purely decorative.

positions.label: The whole image-alternatives goal is the wrong frame
positions.detail: Pushes to revisit his "Meaningful images have a text alternative" proposal against the current draft's goal that users have equivalent alternatives for images (#272). Cites WebAIM's finding that nearly a third of images on popular home pages have missing, questionable or repetitive alternative text, and argues there is no agreement on what an "equivalent" even is — ask ten experts and get ten answers. Wants a more scalable, consistent approach that works without technology changes and adapts as technology shifts, and points to slides 11-17 of an earlier working-group presentation on inter-rater reliability.

agreed: "Detectable" as currently written is ambiguous — WilcoFiers and JasonAment reach that conclusion independently, and iadawn's confusion about how it could be foundational is the same complaint from a different angle.
Presence of an img element does not establish that an image is non-decorative — mraccess77's answer to MakotoUeki was unrebutted.
The detectable/decorative collision in #357 was resolved by the drafting changes in PR 414 and the issue is closed.
open: Whether the requirement is defined or deleted — WilcoFiers wants it dropped, JasonAment wants a normative definition, and no one has replied to either.
Whether "non-decorative images" should be restated as "images that convey meaning", as MakotoUeki proposes in #467.
Whether the test is split into code-inspection and non-code-inspection branches, and whether an accessibility API check sits between code and screen reader as mraccess77 suggests (#606).
mbgower's request in #272 for the group to revisit his alternative proposal drew no response in the thread.
summary.note: Six threads but only six comments across all of them: most of these are single unanswered review filings rather than exchanges. #357 is the one thread that ran to a conclusion, and it closed as resolved by drafting rather than by argument.

summary.headline: Not a debate so much as one proposal being sharpened: whether prepared sign language translation for prerecorded media should be a named requirement rather than an aspiration, and how far beyond video it should reach.

positions.label: Name it, require it, and it will build its own supply
positions.detail: Argues WCAG 2.0 put sign language at AAA and implementation collapsed as a result; writing as a Deaf person, InfoGapBuster reports that when sign language is not a required criterion organisations default to captions alone (#325). Wants "provision of videos with sign language translation" defined as a distinct Outcome, and draws a line the draft does not: interpretation is real-time signing for live contexts, translation is prepared in advance with attention to clarity and accuracy, and translation is what prerecorded content intended for repeated viewing by a wide audience should get. Answers the obvious objection about scarce qualified interpreters and translators by arguing that requiring it generates demand, expands the pool, and accumulates data that could train future AI translation.

positions.label: Go further — signed alternatives for text, not just media
positions.detail: Agrees with the whole proposal but wants Gold treated as a genuine aspirational benchmark, and calls for a supplemental requirement that sign language users have access to a sign language alternative for website text, not only for video. Grounds it in anti-discrimination law rather than practice: the UDHR, ICCPR, EU Charter and American Convention, plus the ADA's auxiliary-aids duty, the BSL Act 2022 and BSL (Scotland) Act 2015, Ireland's Irish Sign Language Act 2017, South Korea's Korean Sign Language Act 2016, New Zealand's NZSL Act 2006, and Filipino Sign Language mandates. Adds ISO 24495-1:2023, ISO/IEC 29184:2020, GDPR Article 12(1) and EU AI Act Articles 14 and 50 on information in an intelligible, preferred-language form.

positions.label: Nothing can be pinned to a level yet
positions.detail: The only note of caution in the thread. Gold is likely achievable without meeting everything listed at that level, and the working group has not finalised what any of Bronze, Silver or Gold mean, so nothing definitive can be said about placing sign language in one. Neither participant contested this, and both continued proposing level assignments.

agreed: Captions and sign language are not interchangeable — for users whose first language is signed, written captions do not deliver full comprehension. Unrebutted throughout.
The interpretation/translation distinction is real and the current draft does not make it; prepared translation is the right fit for prerecorded content.

InfoGapBuster's revised framework after md84419's intervention: sign language alternatives for text are not required at Bronze, recommended at Silver, and expected for key information such as policy documents, educational materials and terms of service at Gold.
open: Whether sign language for prerecorded media stays supplemental or becomes a required criterion — InfoGapBuster's central ask, which nobody has answered.
Whether the scope extends from multimedia to website text at all, as md84419 proposes.

Where this belongs in the document — md84419 notes in November 2025 that the issue is filed under Image and Media Alternatives but is really about text alternatives, and probably needs a new section under Text and Wording.
summary.note: A single thread (#325) with six comments, and effectively a conversation between two people who agree, with one procedural caution from GreggVan. There is no opposing camp on record here — the proposal has not been rejected, it has not been taken up either.

summary.headline: Whether live sign language interpretation belongs in WCAG 3 as an organisational assertion at all, or should be a supplemental requirement — asked once, answered by nobody, and closed.

positions.label: Wrong instrument for the job
positions.detail: Questions whether "We provide sign language interpretation for all live audio content" should be a supplemental requirement rather than an assertion (#471). An assertion is a statement of organisational policy that a conformance claim carries, not something testable against the content; the implication is that live interpretation is a content outcome and should be stated as one. Filed in December 2025 with no body beyond the question, no comments, and closed in June 2026.

positions.label: Interpretation is the live half of a two-part gap
positions.detail: In #325, distinguishes sign language interpretation — real-time signing used in live contexts — from translation prepared in advance, and argues the draft does not separate them. Places live interpretation at Silver where appropriate, and at Gold as high-quality interpretation with cultural and linguistic appropriateness alongside multilingual captions. Writing as a Deaf person, argues that anything short of a defined requirement leaves organisations relying on captions alone, and that requiring it is what builds the currently limited pool of qualified interpreters.

positions.label: Rest it on language-discrimination law
positions.detail: Supports the proposal and pushes past it, calling for a supplemental requirement that sign language users have a signed alternative for website text. Cites jurisdictions that already mandate live interpreting or translation in public services: the ADA's auxiliary aids and services duty for US public entities, the UK's BSL Act 2022, BSL (Scotland) Act 2015 and Equality Act 2010, Ireland's Irish Sign Language Act 2017, South Korea's Korean Sign Language Act 2016, New Zealand's NZSL Act 2006, and Filipino Sign Language mandates — framing signed access as a reasonable adjustment rather than an enhancement.

positions.label: Level placement is premature
positions.detail: Gold is probably achievable without meeting everything at that level, and none of Bronze, Silver or Gold has been finalised, so no definitive statement about placing sign language in a level is possible yet. Unrebutted; the thread continued assigning levels anyway.

agreed: Live interpretation and prepared translation are distinct things the current draft does not distinguish — InfoGapBuster's framing drew no objection.
The conformance levels are not settled, which limits what any of these proposals can actually claim (GreggVan).
Captions alone do not give equitable access to Deaf users whose first language is signed.
open: Whether this stays an assertion or becomes a supplemental requirement — MakotoUeki's #471 question never received a substantive answer on the record.
Whether live sign language interpretation becomes a required criterion rather than a policy statement, which is InfoGapBuster's underlying ask in #325.
md84419's observation that #325 is filed under Image and Media Alternatives but is really about text alternatives, and probably needs a new section under Text and Wording.
summary.note: #471 was closed in June 2026 with zero comments, so the assertion-versus-supplemental question that is most specific to this provision was resolved somewhere other than the issue thread. Everything else here comes from #325, a multi-provision proposal where live interpretation is one label among six.
