Requirements: Non-text Contrast

summary.headline: Whether a visual state requirement should be tied to programmatic state, and whether disabled controls keep their exemption from contrast, get a mandated indicator, or simply stop being classed as non-interactive.

positions.label: States must be visually distinct and match the programmatic state
positions.detail: The draft SC in #193 reads: when a user interface component visibly indicates its states, these states are visually distinct and correspond to the programmatic states. The wording deliberately dodges the question the mobile accessibility task force could not settle — how much visual difference counts, since changing one pixel in a graphic is technically a difference — and instead leans on 1.4.11 to handle the 3:1 contrast of the salient part. The value he claims for it is the correspondence itself: catching a state change that is missing, reversed, or otherwise out of sync.

positions.label: Keep it visual; programmatic state is 4.1.2's job
positions.detail: Mixing programmatic state into a visual SC opens a loophole: a control with no programmatic state fails 4.1.2, but would nominally pass this one because there is nothing to disagree with. He proposed replacing that clause with wording along the lines of accurately represents the current state of the component, and also questioned whether visually distinct is firm enough for normative language, foreseeing the same problems as visible focus indication. detlevhfischer accepted the substitution as an improvement.

positions.label: Disabled controls need contrast or a disabled icon
positions.detail: #197 starts from the observation that disabled interface elements work badly for people with low vision and that exempting them from 1.4.3 was the wrong fix; DavidMacDonald proposes at least 3:1 contrast OR an icon marking the element disabled. bkimmel seconds the problem, particularly where disabled controls are used to advertise the potential of an interaction — fill these fields in and you can submit — which he calls a huge safe harbour for things that cut against the Perceivable goal. He is not convinced an icon specifically is the answer.

positions.label: Contrast yes, mandated icons no
positions.detail: He would far rather see some form of minimum contrast apply, to solve readability, than require an icon — WCAG cannot start demanding icons everywhere without dictating visual design. His preferred shape is a more general intent of indicating that something is disabled, and he flags a crossover with how user agents themselves render disabled state.

positions.label: The definitions exclude the elements in question
positions.detail: Reviewing #197 against the current draft, adampage notes disabled elements fall outside the definition of interactive element — an element that responds to user input and has a distinct programmatically determinable name — so the neighbouring Interactive elements distinguishable provision does not reach them. They appear instead to match non-interactive element (does not respond to user input and does not include sub-parts), but are absent from that definition's examples and notes, so the intent is unclear. He suggests broadening the term or introducing a new one for elements that exist to be interactive even when conditionally disabled or read-only, and points at the Disabled controls explained provision and w3c/wcag#5053 as related.

positions.label: Split contrast by luminance, hue and spatial frequency
positions.detail: #207 proposes reorganising all the colour and contrast outcomes on vision-science lines: luminance carries high spatial frequency information and is what reading depends on, hue matters for object recognition and colour-coded non-text material, and spatial frequency — font weight, size, letter and line spacing, padding, glyph design — is the critical factor in readability. That yields two guidelines, one for not relying on colour alone plus non-text contrast, one for luminance contrast in readable content, with non-text use cases classified as Semantic, Symbolic, DataViz and Container. He also argues specific legacy numbers are unsupported: the 80-characters-per-line figure traces to IBM equipment economics rather than research (Bringhurst's 66 characters, or a 50 to 70 range, offered as informative), and a 1.5 line-height rule is near meaningless in CSS because the x-height to font-size ratio varies by 50 percent or more between families.

agreed: The programmatic-states clause in the #193 draft should go. detlevhfischer accepted patrickhlauke's alternative framing and nobody returned to defend the original.

Micro-SC proliferation is a real risk — detlevhfischer dreads the proliferation of bitty SCs that interact in multiple ways, as 2.4.7 and 1.4.11 already do, and patrickhlauke would rather see a few chunky, well thought-out SCs than a goldrush for 2.2. Their tentative answer was a wider provision covering interface components being visible and their states discernible.
Exempting disabled controls from contrast entirely is a problem for low-vision users; the disagreement is only over the remedy.
Both #193 and #197 need more research — alastc took each off the WCAG 2.2 slate on the same day in July 2020 for that reason, unopposed.
open: Whether disabled elements should be brought inside the definition of interactive element, given a new term, or explicitly named in the non-interactive element notes — adampage raised all three and has had no reply.
Whether a state-change requirement can be written testably at all, which is detlevhfischer's original one-pixel question and patrickhlauke's doubt about visually distinct as normative language.
Whether #193 stays in the repository, moves to WCAG 3 proper, or is deleted. patrickhlauke asked alastc directly in August 2024 and the question is still unanswered.
Whether the contrast outcomes get restructured along Myndex's luminance/hue/spatial-frequency split. Nobody has responded to #207.

Whether the requirement is discharged by author styles or by user-agent defaults for interactive items with a background or border — alastc lists it in #270 as a supplemental item without resolving it.
summary.note: This provision is assembled from four threads with very little live discussion. The substantive exchange in #193 is from 2019 and the exchange in #197 from 2019 and 2020, with adampage's 2026 comment the only recent analysis; #207 and #270 are both long structural proposals that have drawn no comments at all, so nothing in them has been tested by rebuttal.

summary.headline: Whether the visual gap between a label and the control it labels can be written as a testable numeric requirement at all — argued out on one 2019 thread while the two issues about accessible names themselves sit unanswered.

positions.label: Iterate until the gap is measurable
positions.detail: Proposed "Label gaps" in #194: when one element acts as a label of another, the gap between them is no larger than twice the smaller of the labelled element's width or height, measurable with a browser ruler or a script comparing absolute positions. When textareas broke that formula he reworked it to four times the smaller dimension of the label itself, so an icon or short text label sets the budget rather than a large field. He cites repeated findings in his own user testing with low vision users — drop-down menus on accessuse.eu and the incobs tablet tests — while conceding the label-to-control pair catches only a subset of the proximity problem, and that the exception list may grow until the requirement is lost, as happened with target size.

positions.label: Any arbitrary line will be gamed and cannot be justified
positions.detail: Found the loophole immediately: a designer could make fields unnecessarily tall purely to buy leeway to push the label further away, conforming while defeating the point for low vision users. detlevhfischer answered "not likely to happen"; patrickhlauke replied that creative interpretations of normative text to do the minimum necessary to pass are routine. His broader position is that layout and design questions resist rigid binary pass/fail rules, that Apple's own iOS guidance is couched as could and should and Apple ignores it freely, and that this belongs in a non-normative best-practice note or at AAA rather than as a hard requirement. He also asked that the measurement drop mm for px to avoid reopening the CSS-versus-physical-units confusion, which detlevhfischer did immediately.

positions.label: Do not fail a common pattern without evidence
positions.detail: awkawk points to left-aligned label columns with aligned fields, where varying label lengths necessarily produce varying gaps, and argues this is common enough that the working group needs clear evidence before proposing a criterion against it — this is not an absolute like page title or programmatic label association. He wants the goal stated first: at what magnification must the user see the full label and the full input, or the full label and part of the input, and what happens when the label is long. jake-abma checked with designers and reported back that almost all current forms would fail the proposed calculation, which he called too prescriptive for design aesthetics, and later that mixed 3x and 4x width-or-height measurements are simply too complicated for designers, developers and testers.

positions.label: Commonality is not correctness, and the evidence already exists
positions.detail: Answers awkawk that clear evidence only ever comes from research, and the group has a chicken-and-egg problem when practitioner experience outruns formal study. Cites the Understanding document for SC 3.3.2, which stated in 2008 that labels in close proximity assist screen magnifier users because field and label are more likely to be visible within the magnified area, plus technique G162 and two Nielsen Norman Group articles on closeness of actions to objects and form white space. Turns the evidence demand back on existing criteria by questioning whether page titles are still demonstrably useful when browsers truncate or hide them. Calls awkawk's own screenshot a prime example of the problem: a common pattern is not thereby a correct one.

positions.label: Reframe it as a viewport test instead of a ruler
positions.detail: patrickhlauke suggested a minimum built on reflow rather than ratios: the related element must be at least partly present in the viewport even at 320 CSS px width. jake-abma picked this up as the direction most likely to work — label and input visible in a 320 CSS px viewport at the same time, easy to test, with exceptions. He also supplied its limits: whether the label is visible depends on how far you have scrolled, something can be inside the viewport and still too far to read, and desktop zoom tools push the label off to the right and force horizontal scrolling, so the desktop case stays unsolved.

positions.label: Widen the scope, or leave the gap to AT
positions.detail: alastc showed the formula failing a usable pattern — the GOV.UK Design System text input with hint text between label and field, and again when an error message is inserted — then proposed folding associated information into the definition of label, and a looser framing that two related things must be close to each other unless there is a programmatic relationship, with gestalt principles consulted for what close means. He intended the escape hatch to leave room for a future user agent that draws an arrow or indicator, and suggested the COGA task force's design guidance as the better home. patrickhlauke rejected both halves: if the requirement is visual then a programmatic relationship is irrelevant to a user who is not running AT that exposes it, shifting the burden to user agents is a cop-out, and since programmatic association is already required by 1.3.1 and usually 4.1.2, a criterion satisfiable by passing those is redundant. jake-abma agreed on widening, arguing all name-value pairs and many other related pairs deserve the same treatment.

agreed: That proximity between related information matters for low vision and magnifier users was never disputed — awkawk states plainly that the concept is clear and everyone can see how it impacts people, and mraccess77's citation of the 2008 SC 3.3.2 Understanding text and G162 drew no rebuttal. The disagreement is entirely about whether "how close is close enough" can be drawn as a line.

The problem is not specific to form labels. patrickhlauke asked whether any two insufficiently close related elements cause the same problem for low vision and zoom users, and jake-abma agreed, extending it to all name-value pairs — neither treated label-and-input as the natural boundary.
Measurement should use CSS px, not mm; detlevhfischer changed the draft on patrickhlauke's first comment.
The first formula does not survive real components — textareas break it (detlevhfischer), and hint text or an inserted error message between label and field break it (alastc). Both were conceded.
open: Whether "Relationships detectable" must stay limited to programmatic relationships or could additionally require visually clear ones — adampage raised this in #194 in May 2026, pointing at #175; patrickhlauke's only reply was that defining how to represent something visually "clearly" lands you in arbitrary graphic design statements. Nothing else followed.

tallneil's #93: whether the provision should require labels to remain visible "at all times" or "in all states" so the label survives after a value is set, and whether it should say explicitly that a placeholder attribute or the first option in a select are not sufficient substitutes for a label. Opened June 2024, no replies.

mraccess77's #184: whether a button's accessible name must carry its context — an "Add" button beside a person's name is visually related but not programmatically — and whether that is a failure of 1.3.1, of 2.4.6, or of neither. He notes buttons are unlike links in that they rarely sit inside a sentence and may act on a whole group of fields, so the link-context reasoning does not transfer, and asks where the line for buttons is drawn. Deferred from w3c/wcag#168 in 2016, still no replies.
What magnification level any metric is meant to serve, and whether the target is seeing the full label plus the full input or only part of it — awkawk's questions, never answered.

Exceptions for table labels, row and column headers together, and legends that sit far from their fields — raised by jake-abma citing mbgower's label-in-name issues. anevins12 asked in 2022 whether that meant spreadsheet-style grids or all tables and got no reply.
Whether this belongs in WCAG as a normative requirement at all, or in COGA design guidance or a separate best-practice document — raised by patrickhlauke and echoed by alastc.
summary.note: The activity is lopsided. All 33 comments sit on #194, and 32 of them were written in a two-week burst in March and April 2019; anevins12's 2022 question went unanswered and the thread was dormant for seven years until adampage revived it in May 2026. The two issues that actually concern accessible names — tallneil's #93 and mraccess77's #184, itself a deferral from 2016 — have never received a single reply.

summary.headline: No discussion of this provision on its own terms — the single labelled thread is a 2019 issue about disabled controls, which reaches this provision only through adampage's closing comment that the definition of interactive element excludes disabled elements.

positions.label: The definition of interactive element leaves disabled controls out
positions.detail: The provision requires interactive elements to be visually distinguishable from static content without interaction and to include visual cues on how to use them, but the defined term covers only elements that respond to user input and have a distinct programmatically determinable name. Disabled elements therefore fall outside it and instead match non-interactive element, an element that does not respond to user input and does not include sub-parts. Because disabled elements are not named in the example or notes around that definition, adampage asks what the group intends and suggests broadening the term, or adding a new one, for elements that exist to be interactive but may conditionally be disabled or read-only. Links w3c/wcag#5053 as related.

positions.label: Underlying ask in #197: mark disabled controls perceivably
positions.detail: DavidMacDonald opened #197 in 2019 proposing that disabled UI elements meet 3:1 contrast or carry a disabled icon, since WCAG 2 exempts them from 1.4.3 and that hurts low-vision users. bkimmel seconded the problem — disabled states used to advertise future interaction create a large safe harbour — while doubting an icon is the answer. patrickhlauke preferred a minimum contrast plus a general intent of indicating disabled state, arguing WCAG cannot start demanding icons everywhere, and noted a possible crossover with user agents' own disabled styling.

agreed: Nothing about this provision's own wording has been settled here; the only substantive claim on record, adampage's reading of the two definitions, is unrebutted.
open: Whether the definition of interactive element should be broadened, or a new term introduced, to cover conditionally disabled and read-only controls — adampage's question, unanswered since May 2026.
alastc took #197 off the WCAG 2.2 slate in 2020 as needing more research, and it has not been picked back up in substance.
summary.note: This provision is exploratory and shares its only thread with "Disabled controls explained" and "Interactive element contrast sufficient"; it has attracted no issue of its own.

summary.headline: Whether a block of content being visually indistinct is an accessibility failure at all, and whether "sufficient surrounding space" can be written as a requirement anyone can test.

positions.label: If it is unclear for everyone, it is not an accessibility problem
positions.detail: Responding to the opening questions in #19, asks whether there is a requirement for blocks and headings to be visually distinct in the first place, since content that is indistinct for every reader alike looks like a design quality issue rather than an accessibility one. His bar is that things be programmatically different. He also rejects the "sufficient semantics" framing as read, on the grounds that WCAG cannot require authors who write meaningless headings to rewrite them to be meaningful.

positions.label: Block structure is a contrast problem, not a styling preference
positions.detail: Argues visual hierarchy is squarely an accessibility issue for COGA among others, and that it is also a contrast issue: the amount of padding around a text block, line spacing and letter spacing all change perceived contrast, and this is most critical for blocks of body text. Contends the primary driver of perceived contrast is spatial, chiefly rasterized font weight, because weight sets the spatial frequency the contrast sensitivity function responds to. Cites Lovie-Kitchin and colleagues for contrast reserve figures keyed to use case, roughly 20 times the JND threshold for article body text down to 3 times for non-fluent spot reading.

positions.label: Catalogue what already works before writing a rule
positions.detail: Wants the methods currently used to separate blocks and headings surveyed first, so a new requirement does not accidentally outlaw one that works, and notes that distinctions are frequently used in combination rather than singly. Lists boldness, font size, typeface, indentation, underlines and overlines, italicization, small caps, script, color, textual or iconographic markers and text alignment. Refines Myndex's three-way split into four groups: spatial, visual text attributes, content and external indicators.

positions.label: Split the visual requirement from the programmatic one
positions.detail: Opened #476 arguing that the visual and programmatic aspects of meaningful content blocks may need to be separate requirements, because one can be satisfied while the other is not. Also asks for "sufficient surrounding space" to be defined, and for exceptions to be considered where a particular layout choice makes added spacing inappropriate.

positions.label: "Sufficient" is subjective and the requirement inverts the visual and the programmatic
positions.detail: Points carried into #476 for review: the draft requires information to be programmatically determinable that is not visually determinable, which reverses the usual direction, and the wording needs to say that where content appears as a block carrying semantic meaning, that block also has to be programmatically determinable. On spacing, paragraphs often have no more space between them than between the lines inside them, yet they are meaningful blocks, so the reductio is whether every document must now add space between every paragraph, and whether the answer is one pixel, two, or three.

agreed: Color alone should not be the distinguishing factor. u9000-Nine is content not to count color as a distinction despite it being common practice and the Word default; Myndex clarifies color is genuinely useful but must accompany weight, size and family rather than carry the distinction on its own, since perception of color varies enormously even among standard vision and shifts with context.

Relative size is a legitimate distinction, absolute size is not. u9000-Nine proposed that a heading being larger than the body text, whatever size that is, should count; Myndex agreed font size is and should be a distinguishing feature.

Font weight belongs with the spatial and contrast group rather than with font styling, because weight determines spatial frequency and therefore perceived contrast. u9000-Nine accepted the reclassification.
GreggVan's baseline that the distinctions at least have to be programmatically different went unchallenged.
open: Whether visual distinctness of blocks is in scope at all. GreggVan asked in September 2023 and nobody in the thread answered him.
What "sufficient surrounding space" means and whether a number can be attached to it. giacomo-petri opened #476 specifically on this; the paragraph-spacing reductio quoted there is unanswered.
Whether visual and programmatic block structure should be one requirement or two (giacomo-petri, #476), and what exceptions exist where a layout choice makes spacing unnecessary.

Where text decoration sits. u9000-Nine asked why it appears under both layout and non-text; Myndex left it open, leaning non-text when it indicates function such as an underlined link and layout when it is merely divisional.

Whether container behaviour under large text zoom belongs to this provision. Myndex wants the smallest body text scalable to roughly 80 to 92 px, an x-height near 42 px and a zoom of 450 to 500 percent, with already-larger text scaling by a smaller percentage, and notes 500 percent is untenable on a phone so device media queries are needed.
summary.note: The nine comments here all come from #19, which is labelled for this provision and for Heading structure available, so the taxonomy work is shared between the two. Substantively it is a two-person exchange between Myndex and u9000-Nine over six weeks in late 2023 that converged on a classification but never produced proposed requirement text; WilcoFiers's opening questions and GreggVan's scope challenge were never resolved, and #476 reopens the same ambiguities two years later with no replies yet.

summary.headline: Whether the provision should police how headings look as well as how they are marked up, and what the heading hierarchy has to be for content that does not naturally have one.

positions.label: Semantics yes, appearance no
positions.detail: Questions whether there is a requirement for headings to be visually distinct at all, since headings that are not distinct for anyone are not obviously an accessibility question. Accepts differentiating font from typeface as long as the result is programmatically different. Pushes back on the suggestion that sufficient semantics on headings matters more than visual presentation, reading "sufficient semantics" as "sufficient meaning" and arguing WCAG cannot require authors who write meaningless headings to rewrite them.

positions.label: Visual hierarchy is an accessibility issue and a contrast issue
positions.detail: Holds that content structure for a good visual hierarchy matters for COGA among others, and that it is simultaneously a contrast question: padding around a heading, leading and letter spacing all change perceived contrast, as does font weight. Argues weight is the most critical spatial quality because it sets the spatial frequency that drives contrast sensitivity, illustrated with same-color samples at different weights placed on the contrast sensitivity curve. Also warns that the CSS font-size metric is close to futile as an absolute, since size and weight vary massively between families.

positions.label: Enumerate the distinctions in use before restricting any
positions.detail: Wants existing sufficiently distinct methods catalogued so a requirement does not accidentally remove one, and stresses that combinations of distinctions matter. Proposes four groups rather than Myndex's three: spatial, visual text attributes, content, and external indicators, with capitalization, writing system, sentence type and person placed under content. Argues writing system in particular belongs with content, since writing in sitelen pona carries semantics and nuance that Latin script or speech does not.

positions.label: Nesting and a single h1
positions.detail: Filed #81 from a public-agwg-comments email asking for an outcome stating that section heading levels be semantically nested so they form a hierarchical outline of the content, and that there be only one h1 per page, reserved for introducing the main content or topic and matching or closely resembling the page title. No one has replied since May 2024.

positions.label: Fix the terminology and name the exceptions
positions.detail: Opened #478 asking that "higher" and "lower" be replaced when referring to heading levels, since which direction each word points is ambiguous. Also wants "meaningful block of content" clearly defined and exceptions specified, recognising that paragraphs, letters and emails may not require headings, while insisting any exception be explicit enough that it cannot be used as a loophole. Notes both items may resolve from a single consistent definition.

agreed: Font and typeface have to be kept distinct in the spec's language. WilcoFiers's example, that Helvetica 12pt bold and Helvetica italic 14px are different fonts sharing one typeface, drew no objection.
Whatever distinguishes a heading has to be programmatically different, not only visually different. GreggVan's condition went unchallenged.

A heading being larger than the body text is a valid distinction even though an absolute font size is not. u9000-Nine proposed the split and Myndex agreed size is and should remain a distinguishing feature.

Color should not be the sole distinguisher. u9000-Nine is willing not to count it; Myndex agrees it must be an accompaniment rather than the solo distinction, given how far color perception varies with context even for standard vision.
open: How to decide whether headings are sufficiently distinct from each other and from surrounding content, whether color contrast can carry that judgement, and whether reading distance should be a factor. WilcoFiers asked all three in #19 in 2023 and none has been answered.

Whether sufficient semantics on headings matters more than visual distinctness, and whether the visual requirement should simply be that presentation changes away from the default. WilcoFiers raised it, GreggVan contested what it would even mean, and it stalled there.
Whether heading levels must be semantically nested and limited to one h1 per page (rachaelbradley, #81), which has had no discussion at all.

How "meaningful block of content" is defined and which content types are exempt from needing headings (giacomo-petri, #478) - a definition shared with the Blocks of content available (minimum) provision.

Where text decoration belongs. u9000-Nine asked why it sits in both the layout and non-text groups; Myndex left it unresolved, leaning non-text when it signals function and layout when it is merely divisional.
summary.note: Only one of the four threads has any discussion. All nine comments come from #19, which is labelled for this provision and for Blocks of content available (minimum), and is mostly a two-person taxonomy exchange between Myndex and u9000-Nine. #81, #271 and #478 are issue bodies with no replies: #271 is alastc's requirement-tracking issue listing Visually organize content, Regions (Minimum and Enhanced), Section Label, Headings Structure and Programmatic Relationship under one guideline, rather than an argued position.

summary.headline: Whether "relationships detectable" is purely a programmatic requirement, and how to bound it — the two substantive threads behind it are both stalled proposals inherited from WCAG 2.x, one on element nesting and one on visual label proximity.

positions.label: A new provision for role nesting
positions.detail: cstrobbe's proposal in #166 would require that elements used with their native roles be nested according to the content models in their specifications, plus a fourth clause barring links, interactive elements and keyboard-focusable elements as descendants of links. He worked through nineteen numbered code examples showing where a syntax reading of 4.1.1, a validation reading, and the proposal each land — button wrapping an anchor, li inside a div inside a ul, p as a sibling of li, h2 wrapping p. JAWS-test called it exactly what was needed and asked that it also cover ARIA and PDF tags, noting that correct nesting is what lets a screen reader report that a table has 3 columns and 2 rows and that you are in column 2, row 1. JAWS-test cited EN 301 549 clause 11.5.2.9 and Section 508 502.3.7, both of which already require parent-child relationships to be programmatically determinable.

positions.label: Fix or retire 4.1.1 instead of adding a provision
positions.detail: patrickhlauke would rather see 4.1.1 updated normatively in a backwards-compatible way than patch around a poorly interpreted criterion, warning of weird overlaps where one SC is a stricter special case of another. yatil proposes extending 4.1.1 to "markup languages and associated extensions as they relate to accessibility features" and dropping the well-formedness framing from the Understanding document, or alternatively removing 4.1.1 entirely per w3c/wcag#2676. scottaohara agrees: use 4.1.1 for what people think it is for, unless "elements are nested according to their specifications" does not actually mean that. patrickhlauke also argues the singling out of links is arbitrary, since buttons and other controls have the same problem.

positions.label: Do not reinterpret 4.1.1 after the fact
positions.detail: bruce-usab says it is bad to retcon a standard and refuses the "use it for what people think it's for" framing; GreggVan agrees and adds that 4.1.1 should be clarified to mean what the working group meant when it was written, not what people later want it to mean. bruce-usab separately notes the proposal arrived too late for WCAG 2.2. cstrobbe's own reply is that the intents differ: 4.1.1 is about a user agent building an unambiguous parse tree, while his proposal is about name, role, state and value being exposed unambiguously through an accessibility API, which puts it closer to 4.1.2.

positions.label: Measure the label gap
positions.detail: detlevhfischer's #194 proposal caps the gap between a label and the element it labels at twice the smaller of the labelled element's width or height, illustrated with a 16 px-tall field passing at a 32 px gap and failing at 33 px. He later revised it to four times the smaller dimension of the label itself, to escape the problem that the original formula breaks for textarea. mraccess77 defends the need against demands for evidence, pointing out that the SC 3.3.2 Understanding document said in 2008 that labels close to their field help screen-magnifier users, that G162 already exists, and citing Nielsen Norman Group material on proximity and form white space; his answer to "this is a common pattern" is that a common pattern is not necessarily a correct one.

positions.label: The gap metric breaks real designs and lacks evidence
positions.detail: jake-abma checked with designers and reported that almost all current forms would fail and that the calculation is too prescriptive for design aesthetics, and that the measurement scheme — four times, three times, widths, heights, mixed elements — is too complicated for designers, developers and testers alike. awkawk points to the very common pattern of left-aligned labels against aligned fields, where varying label length forces varying gaps, and says disallowing a common pattern requires clear evidence. alastc notes the proposal would fail the GOV.UK Design System text input with hint text, and asks what happens when an error message is inserted. patrickhlauke finds the loophole immediately: a designer could make fields excessively tall purely to buy leeway to push the label further away, defeating the point while passing; he also asks for hard proof that larger gaps harm particular users rather than the working group making things up. detlevhfischer concedes the exception list grows until the original requirement is lost, and that focusing on label-to-control catches only a subset of the proximity problems he has seen in low-vision user testing.

positions.label: The requirement is unbounded as written
positions.detail: In #451 GreggVan argues that if a relationship is not presented to anybody, it is unclear what the requirement is getting at, and that without scoping there are a million ways elements can be related and all of them would have to be conveyed programmatically; he proposes narrowing it to "when relationships of meaning between elements are presented visually, they are also conveyed programmatically." giacomo-petri opened the issue acknowledging the tests are incomplete and that the requirement must either gain sufficient tests or state its applicability clearly. adampage's specific gaps are error messages and help text for form controls, and tables with headers, bodies, footers, data cells and header cells — questions that arise precisely because the written tests are so narrow.

agreed: Validation errors involving no element with a native role cause no accessibility problem — cstrobbe's examples of span wrapping h6 and a span carrying an href attribute fail validation, harm nobody, and went unchallenged as cases the provision should not catch.

Proximity of a label to its control genuinely matters for low-vision and magnifier users; awkawk, the main sceptic on #194, states outright that he does not dispute the concept and that the challenge is only deciding how close is close enough so it can be tested.

A whole class of parent-child relationships is not expressible as element nesting at all — JAWS-test's list of aria-owns, radio buttons grouped by the name attribute, and aria-level on treegrids drew no rebuttal, and cstrobbe conceded the requirement should be framed around what reaches the accessibility API rather than around nesting.
open: Whether the provision stays limited to programmatic relationships or additionally requires visually clear ones. adampage raised it on #194 against the current draft text; patrickhlauke's objection is that defining how to represent something "clearly" in visual terms lands you in arbitrary graphic design statements.
Whether the requirement should apply only where a relationship is presented visually, per GreggVan's proposed rewording in #451.
What the tests must cover: error messages and help text for form controls, and table headers, bodies, footers and cells — adampage's list, carried into #451 by giacomo-petri.

What artefact is evaluated — source code, DOM or accessibility tree. JAWS-test raised this on #166: source often has no bearing after JS and CSS, while DOM and accessibility tree reflect browser repair that is not consistent across browsers, which is why 4.1.1 existed in the first place.

Whether roles overridden by ARIA are in scope, and how to word that technology-independently. This is cstrobbe's own unanswered question on #166; JAWS-test argues ARIA is exactly where the problems are, since it is widely misused, hard to validate and not consistently repaired by browsers.

Whether any testable proximity metric is achievable at all. jake-abma and patrickhlauke floated a reflow-style alternative — label and input both at least partly visible in a 320 CSS px viewport — and jake-abma noted it leaves desktop zoom-tool users, where the label is simply too far right, unaddressed.

Whether a programmatic relationship should serve as an escape hatch from a visual proximity requirement. alastc proposed it; patrickhlauke called it a cop-out that shifts the burden to user agents and makes the provision redundant, since programmatic association is already required by 1.3.1 and in most cases 4.1.2.
summary.note: Both substantive threads are inherited and largely dormant. #194 was opened in 2019 as a WCAG 2.2 proposal, had its real debate over two weeks in March and April 2019, drew one comment in 2022 from anevins12 that went unanswered, then sat untouched until adampage reopened the question in May 2026 against the WCAG 3 draft text. #166 dates from 2022 and its last exchange is bruce-usab and GreggVan on retconning, with cstrobbe's promised rewording never posted. #271 is alastc's requirement-tracking stub listing five requirements and a Google doc link, with no discussion at all.

summary.headline: Whether a requirement that headings describe topic or purpose can survive content that has no topic — fiction, irony, chapter numbers — and whether the fix is new normative wording or an Understanding note, given that any loosening also loosens the requirement on form labels.

positions.label: The normative wording has no room for fiction
positions.detail: 2.4.6 says headings must describe the purpose or topic; it does not say only where a specific topic exists, nor that a heading may merely label a section (#170). A chapter heading might set a mood or theme, or introduce levity or absurdity, and the examples in the Understanding document reinforce the bias by showing content that breaks down neatly by topic. He has always ignored the SC for publishing, but calls it troubling to tell people to ignore a criterion because it does not make sense outside one context, especially as the part about labels describing the purpose of inputs is genuinely useful.

positions.label: The wording is wooly, so fiction passes in practice — but irony shows it should not
positions.detail: scottaohara reads a chapter title as naming the chapter you are about to read rather than summarising it, which is itself a useful title, and says he would be surprised to see anyone report this. patrickhlauke agrees more bluntly: determining what is and is not descriptive enough is completely wooly and subjective, so there is plenty of wiggle room, you can handwave fiction, and if someone insists it fails, let a judge or lawyer work it out. He still presses the hard case — a chapter titled A peaceful morning over text describing atrocities in a war-torn country is deliberately non-descriptive, even says the opposite of the content, and appears to contravene the normative requirement, while the Understanding quietly pivots from descriptive to merely providing a cue or landmark. bruce-usab's counter is that headings must describe topic or purpose rather than be descriptive, and that A peaceful morning memorably identifies the chapter's main substance.

positions.label: The intent already covers it; the defect is that you must read Understanding to find that out
positions.detail: His recollection is that fiction chapter titles were among the use cases considered when 2.4.6 was phrased. The Understanding document states that a word, or even a single character, may suffice if it provides an appropriate cue to finding and navigating content — so a cryptic but deliberately chosen chapter title clears the bar, and esoteric novel headings are both descriptive and well suited to their purpose. He concedes a plain reading has the implication mattgarrish describes and calls it a defect that the nuance lives only in Understanding, adding that in publishing the SC is always satisfied because a real-world failure is probably impossible to find, which is not true of the web, where pages with seemingly random headings exist.

positions.label: Do not loosen it, because labels are in the same sentence
positions.detail: JAWS-test opposes rewriting the SC because any relaxation weakens it for labels, and form labels should be meaningful — not ironic, not a single character — even where headings can be held to a lower bar. His preference is an Understanding addition covering fiction now, with WCAG 3 treating headings and labels as separate requirements. mattgarrish accepts this is the cost of combining the two in one criterion. Two replacement phrasings were floated and neither survived: mattgarrish's Headings and labels establish context, which he argued covers chapter numbers that convey no topic but do tell you how far into a book you are, and bruce-usab's Headings and labels provide descriptive identification of the topic or purpose, which mattgarrish rejected as a wordier way of saying describes that still assumes a topic exists.

positions.label: Labelled landmarks as a requirement in their own right
positions.detail: A separate strand (#80), forwarded from a public-agwg-comments email, argues that sections being visually and programmatically distinguishable is not enough and that clearly labelled semantic landmarks separating distinct page content should be required — header, main navigation, breadcrumb navigation, main content, aside, footer. The case made is practical: landmarks are well supported in browsers, easy to implement in HTML5, ARIA and JavaScript, deliver real benefit to AT users, and are easy to test. Nobody has replied.

positions.label: Define the scope before requiring anything
positions.detail: #477 asks for meaningful blocks of content to be defined, quoting GreggVan's objection that the phrase is used to mean a section, a heading and even a paragraph inside a section, and that one term cannot carry three meanings — his test case is whether posting a letter online obliges you to label its introduction and its sections. It also asks that the exception, where a label is not needed to understand the purpose of the content within the context of use, be bounded, since as written it can be invoked too broadly.

agreed: There is genuine tension between the normative text and the Understanding document — bruce-usab concedes the point after arguing the intent is sound.
It would be better if the criterion were clearer about its application; mattgarrish and bruce-usab both say so in nearly the same words.
Changing the shared wording cannot be done without weakening the label half, which is why separating headings from labels in WCAG 3 is the direction both mattgarrish and JAWS-test end up pointing at.
No proposed replacement wording has held up. mattgarrish left it at needing more thought and was content to defer the problem to 3.0.
open: What the replacement phrasing is, if any. bruce-usab explicitly wanted something narrow enough to ship as an erratum and nothing met that bar.

Whether labelled semantic landmarks become a distinct requirement — rachaelbradley's #80 has had no response since it was filed in May 2024, and the issue carries an instruction to reply to the originating email once addressed.
What meaningful blocks of content means and how tightly the context-of-use exception is drawn, raised by giacomo-petri in #477 on GreggVan's behalf.
How Section Label sits against Regions, Headings Structure and Programmatic Relationship, which alastc lists together as requirements in #271 without comment.
summary.note: The only real debate here, #170, is a 2021 argument about WCAG 2.x SC 2.4.6 that has been carried into the WCAG 3 repository as background; it ends unresolved with the participants agreeing to leave it to 3.0. The three other threads — #80, #271 and #477 — have no comments at all, so the landmark, requirement-tracking and definitional questions are on the record but untested.

summary.headline: Five mostly single-comment issues circling one question — whether a rule about clause nesting is feasible, useful and valid outside English — with only chaals and murata2makoto offering substantive argument and neither answered.

positions.label: Too hard for authors without writing resources
positions.detail: julierawe opened #552 carrying a January 2026 survey comment from sydneycolemanfromgoogle that the requirement will be incredibly challenging for parties without dedicated writing support and does not seem to add significantly to understanding. julierawe's answer is procedural and tooling-based: the requirement was moved from core to supplemental after the survey closed, which may resolve part of the concern, and free AI tools already flag complex sentence structures, so WCAG 3 could encourage them to call out nested clauses specifically.

positions.label: Not too hard, but too simplistic
positions.detail: Concedes the requirement takes real work and is very hard without someone who works on language, but notes few sites have nobody working on content, so difficulty is not the objection. Accepts that removing nested clauses generally does improve understanding, much more so for deep nesting. His actual complaint is that the requirement is too simple to be very useful: it does not differentiate by depth, clear writing is hard to test because people disagree on what is clear, and rules differ between languages so a test built for one is often useless in another.

positions.label: The premise is English-specific
positions.detail: Argues in #569 that clause nesting is not inherently a readability problem. The English centre-embedded example about the rat, the cat and the dog is genuinely hard to process, but the equivalent Japanese structure is unremarkable for native speakers, and the same holds for Korean and other head-final languages. Concludes that the real source of difficulty varies by language — word order ambiguity, unclear referents — and that treating nested clauses as a general problem overgeneralises from English.

positions.label: Editorial fixes to the examples
positions.detail: In #529 sydneycolemanfromgoogle asked whether "aced" should be replaced in a pass example as an idiom that may be hard to translate; hidde changed it to "did well on" in commit b1351ad and closed the issue on merge. In the still-open #530 sydneycolemanfromgoogle notes the listed nesting conjunctions may read as exhaustive when words like "that" also qualify, and supplies a rewritten test procedure making the list open-ended.

agreed: "Aced" was an inappropriate example word and has been replaced in the draft — the only thing actually resolved across these five issues.
Removing nested clauses generally does aid comprehension in English, which chaals grants even while objecting to the requirement's form.
open: Whether moving the requirement from core to supplemental addresses sydneycolemanfromgoogle's feasibility objection — julierawe proposed reaching out to ask and no outcome is recorded.
Whether it should move further, from supplemental to best practice, raised at the February 3rd AG meeting and tracked in #560 with no comments since.
Whether the requirement should account for nesting depth rather than treating any nesting alike (chaals).
Whether the requirement is valid for head-final languages at all (murata2makoto), unanswered since February 2026.
sydneycolemanfromgoogle's proposed non-exhaustive rewording of the conjunction list in #530.
summary.note: #560 summarises an AG meeting rather than hosting discussion: it records unnamed members raising feasibility concerns with specialized content, and another member citing complex sentence structures as a significant cognitive barrier in their own experience. Four of the five issues have zero or one comment.

summary.headline: Whether a maximum contrast ratio should exist, or whether the real variable is screen luminance and the answer is user adjustability instead.

positions.label: Cap the contrast
positions.detail: cawa-93 opens #171 with white text on black at a 21:1 ratio, which passes 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) at AAA and is, in their words, absolutely not readable, and proposes a maximum alongside the minimum. NathanInnes offers Twitter's branding revamp as a case in point: it passed beyond the standard and a lot of users found it difficult to read and straining on the eyes.

positions.label: A cap would harm me — make it adjustable instead
positions.detail: JAWS-test finds high-contrast text readable in itself, accepts that some people struggle with it, and argues the fix is for colour adaptation to user needs to work well and for WCAG to support that adaptability via custom styles, Windows High Contrast Mode and similar. mraccess77 says a contrast maximum would negatively affect them personally while acknowledging others need low contrast, and concedes specific bad combinations exist — small white text on black being one — before asking whether a better calculation than current contrast could isolate those cases, pointing at Myndex's work.

positions.label: The WCAG 2 math cannot carry a maximum
positions.detail: Myndex's objection in #171 is that WCAG 2 contrast math is not perceptually accurate — it already overstates minimum contrast for dark colours — so building a cap on it would produce more unreadable pages, not fewer, and entrench the misunderstanding of how contrast and readability work. Reframes the problem as excess luminance rather than excess ratio: users crank screen brightness to cope with all the low-contrast content in the wild, then get blasted by a site with good contrast. Also notes the OP's own example is too small and too crowded to be evidence. bruce-usab agrees white on black is a common barrier but cannot see how to address it in WCAG 2.x even at AAA, since the same rule would flag plain black-on-white body text, and points to APCA as the WCAG 3 route.

positions.label: There is a maximum, but only in dark mode
positions.detail: The 2023 status update separates the cases: no maximum contrast in light mode, only a maximum luminance, which is a user display control rather than an author one, with paper-emulation best practice of keeping body-text background at about 85 percent of the adaptation state. Dark mode is different — excessively bright text on dark backgrounds causes halation and glare — and names interim experimental values under study of Lc -90 maximum for body text and Lc -85 for larger text, using APCA 0.0.98G4g. Adds that there is room for at least two dark schemes, day and night, and that daltonised, photophobia and Meares-Irlen schemes will likely need their own maxima.

positions.label: Lc -90 is still too much
positions.detail: Reports from a calibrated setup — displays at 150 cd/m2 white luminance, room illuminance around 100 lx, IPS LCD at roughly 1000:1 static contrast — that black on white is comfortable while white on black remains practically unreadable, partly from halation due to astigmatism. Finds Lc -90 uncomfortable and would want something nearer Lc -50 for light-on-dark. Also warns the fix cuts both ways: in a properly calibrated environment, an author lowering contrast for dark text on light backgrounds reduces readability, comparing blue on brown to printing on kraft paper rather than white.

positions.label: User-side colour control, stated plainly
positions.detail: emanser869's #178 proposes adding to 1.4.8 that foreground and background colours can be adjusted by the user to apply uniformity of contrast. utkudyn-a11y's #618 pushes the other direction for a specific case, asking that captions carry at least 4.5:1 between caption text and its background as a core requirement rather than a supplemental adjustability one, because caption legibility directly affects partially sighted users.

agreed: Some specific high-ratio combinations genuinely are hard to read — small white text on black is named by cawa-93, mraccess77 and bruce-usab alike. The dispute is over the remedy, not the symptom.
Users need a way to adapt foreground and background colours to their own needs; JAWS-test, mraccess77 and emanser869 all land here.
Screen brightness set too high is a real contributing cause. kepstin agrees with Myndex on this even while disagreeing about the threshold.
WCAG 2.x contrast math is the wrong instrument for a maximum; nobody defended using it that way.
open: Whether a maximum contrast value should be normative at all, and for which modes. Myndex's dark-mode-only framing is the most developed answer and has drawn one substantive response.
Where the dark-mode maximum sits. kepstin's lived report of Lc -50 is roughly 40 Lc away from the Lc -90 under study, and nobody has reconciled the two.
How to raise readability for users on too-bright displays without cutting contrast below what users with correctly calibrated displays need — kepstin states this as an unsolved trade-off.
Whether peak-luminance choice for a given dark scheme is a user display responsibility or an author one, which Myndex flags as open and complicated by ambient light and device output range.

What "high-contrast" means in the provision's own tests, which reference a high-contrast light-on-dark theme and a high-contrast dark-on-light theme without defining the term. julierawe asked this in #501.
utkudyn-a11y's proposal to make a 4.5:1 caption-background ratio a core requirement.
summary.note: The discussion is almost entirely #171, and much of it is old — the substantive exchange runs 2021 to 2023 with a single 2025 reply from kepstin. #178, #501 and #618 are unanswered issue bodies; julierawe's definitional question in #501 is short, central to testing this provision, and has no response at all.

threads.title: Color and Contrast For Text & Non-Text Outcomes
Requirements: Text appearance
Rendering‑aware contrast model proposal for WCAG 3

summary.headline: Whether a higher contrast threshold buys anything once text is past contrast constancy, and whether "enhanced" should be a conformance level at all rather than a second threshold keyed to what the text is for.

positions.label: Above contrast constancy, more contrast is the wrong lever
positions.detail: Myndex builds the enhanced case on Lovie-Kitchin's critical contrast, the point past which further increases in text-to-background contrast produce no improvement in reading speed or comprehension. Once a design reaches that Lc level it enters contrast constancy, and from there the spatial factors — whitespace, stroke weight, size, crowding — govern readability, with the perceived luminance difference ranking, in his words, among the least important. He cites Chung and Tjan for the mechanism: reading speed shows strong spatial-frequency dependence when text contrast is low, which is to say the payoff from added contrast is conditional on size and weight rather than additive to them. sdw32's glance study supplies the matching data point at enhanced-tier levels, with Open Sans Extra Bold at APCA Lc 30 outperforming Open Sans Light at Lc 75 (the weight-quantification method behind it is covered under text-contrast-sufficient-minimum).

positions.label: Dissolve the level into a use-case taxonomy
positions.detail: Myndex's #207 restructure folds 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) and 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) into one guideline, "Visually readable content uses ample luminance contrast," and re-cuts the requirement by what the text is doing rather than by tier. His categories are FLUENT — high-fluent body text, defined as more than two continuous lines in a block or column at an x-height of about 16px or less, fluent text up to two and a half lines, and large fluent headers above about 32px — and SUB-FLUENT, covering soft readability, spot readability (readable with fixation), logo and branding colours, and incidental text in images. GreggVan arrives at the same shape from the opposite direction, proposing a text visibility tool with one pass threshold X for running text and a different X for menus, buttons and other short strings where the reader has time to fixate. Neither treats the higher requirement as a conformance level; both treat it as a function of use case.

positions.label: Magnification already is the enhanced level
positions.detail: GreggVan's position is that if a size is large enough for typical vision, then that size under magnification is good enough for low vision — large print for typical viewers is large print for low vision users, fine print is fine print, and anyone with very low vision has magnification built into every OS. He adds that stating any floor would require specifying screen size and CSS pitch, which the author does not control, and says a lot of thought went into concluding there is no way to guarantee text is never too small. Applied to the enhanced provision this removes its reason to exist: the higher tier is delivered by the user's zoom rather than by the author's default presentation.

positions.label: Zoom has a ceiling, so the higher tier has to be in the default
positions.detail: sdw32 rejects the premise of typical vision outright — vision is a bell curve like grip strength, and he routinely measures young people at 20/10, twice the 20/20 reference. Since designers default to designing for themselves, a site built by a 20/10 designer accommodates only 20/50 at the browser maximum of 500% zoom, which he does not accept as maximising foreseeable use. Working backwards from 20/200 access at 500% gives a target of 20/40 suitability at 100%, which is his 8 CSS px x-height floor. On GreggVan's pitch objection he answers that no screen pitch need be specified, only the CSS px definition itself — 96 DPI viewed at 28 inches or 711mm, implying 427mm for a 160 DPI phone — and offers a live failure, the string "achetés = 30% d'économies" on carrefour.fr, as text that fails EN 301 549 while passing the current WCAG 3 draft. The minimum-level half of this exchange is covered under text-contrast-sufficient-minimum and text-style-readable-minimum.

positions.label: The real enhanced requirement is triggered by circumstance, not by tier
positions.detail: EN 301 549 v4.1.0, which sdw32 worked on, already ships the two-level structure but keys it to whether the text can be enlarged rather than to a conformance level. Zoomable text gets a best-practice x-height of at least 8 CSS px, corresponding to 1.2mm at a 400mm viewing distance with no zooming or screen scaling; text and images of text necessary for all functionality that is closed to text enlargement get at least 16 CSS px of x-height, an exact doubling. His companion weight rule is likewise two-sided rather than a floor: body text between regular-weight and semi-bold Open Sans, and keywords or short phrases neither thinner than regular Open Sans nor heavier than extra-bold, which cuts against reading an enhanced level as simply more.

positions.label: The gold level is defined by a clinical target, not by a multiple
positions.detail: APC-RC carries silver and gold levels with reference fonts a designer matches their own typeface against, and Myndex states the selected contrasts for both are intended to serve a Pelli-Robson score down to 1, a profound contrast deficit on a scale where 2 is normal and lower is worse. That makes the higher tier an answer to a measured population rather than a round multiple of the minimum. nakano0949-web pressed him in #590 on whether a physical contrast model can capture colour vision deficiency and low vision at all; Myndex answered that APCA already improves on WCAG 2 for protans, that a protan compensator pre-shaping luminances for colours with high red primary content is due this year, and that SACAM, an accessibility-adjustable colour model for dynamic personalisation, is in progress. In #207 he notes the same physics already rejects pure red against black or dark colours, since red on black is poor for standard vision too.

agreed: Luminance contrast and the spatial properties of text are not independent levers. Myndex's framing that contrast sensitivity is dictated by spatial frequency, which he calls peer-reviewed consensus dating to Stevens 1961 and Bartleson and Breneman 1967, drew no rebuttal in either thread where he raised it.

Not everything in a view should be at maximum contrast or maximum size. Myndex argues variation is required for visual hierarchy and for cognitive accessibility in particular, and GreggVan's separate thresholds for running text and for short strings reach the same conclusion from the testability side — the two main antagonists converge here.

Whatever the enhanced requirement asks for has to be anchored in x-height rather than font-size. sdw32 states he absolutely agrees with Myndex on this; the ratios that make font-size uninstructive are 0.55 for Verdana, 0.52 for Arial and Helvetica and 0.45 for Times New Roman. teohhanhui's correction that CSS already has the ex unit was answered by Myndex — ex is a length unit, not a way to set rendered glyph size, which is what the font-x-size proposal in csswg-drafts#6709 exists for — and teohhanhui did not press it.

Myndex's zoom arithmetic went unchallenged: 200% only reaches accommodation for 20/40, body text should be able to reach 400%, meaning 16px scaling to 64px and 48px headline text to 128px, and gains reverse beyond about 2 degrees of visual angle as reading speed falls off.
open: Whether a separate enhanced level should exist at all. Myndex's #207 proposal to dissolve it into the fluent and sub-fluent taxonomy has sat since February 2023 with no comment from anyone.

What the enhanced threshold actually is. No participant in any of the three threads proposes or defends a numeric value for it. sdw32's Lc 30, 45, 60 and 75 are study conditions rather than proposals, and APC-RC's gold level is named but never given a value.

alastc's requirement list in #266 opens with "Maximum text contrast: the rendered text against its background meets a maximum contrast ratio test for its text appearance," and no one in the thread's twenty-plus comments addressed the maximum. Myndex's argument against uniform maximum contrast bears on it but never names it.

Whether an enhanced threshold stated in CSS colour values survives rendering at the sizes where it matters. nakano0949-web's measurements in #590 show anti-aliasing impact climbing sharply below 14px and dominating at 12px and below; only patrickhlauke and Myndex replied.
Whether the protan compensator and SACAM change the enhanced-level answer once released. Both were described as forthcoming in April 2026 and neither is out.

sdw32's pixel-density method for quantifying font weight was put to the group with three explicit questions — is everyone happy with the approach, does a public-domain algorithm exist, and will anyone reimplement it outside VBA to check his numbers. He asked on 20 January 2026 and re-asked on 10 February tagging Myndex and GreggVan by name. Neither answered.

Whether any of this transfers beyond Latin scripts. tsmd's closing comment in #266 is that x-height does not directly apply to Japanese, Chinese or Korean; Myndex's own note that Japanese mixes thin-stroked logographic Kanji with thicker syllabic Kana on the same line means a single spatial threshold is already strained within one writing system.
summary.note: There is no discussion specific to the enhanced level. All three threads carry both the minimum and enhanced provision labels, and every substantive exchange in them is about the floor — whether a minimum exists, what unit it uses, how weight is quantified. #207, the only thread that engages the enhanced level structurally, was opened by Myndex in February 2023 as a survey item, was last updated in May 2026, carries six provision labels including graphical object, interactive element, focus indicator and pointer contrast, and has never received a single comment.

threads.title: Contrast Research: APCA Peer Reviews + Defining a Visual Contrast Guideline
Color and Contrast For Text & Non-Text Outcomes
Requirements: Text appearance
Rendering‑aware contrast model proposal for WCAG 3

summary.headline: Whether the minimum test should be a contrast ratio at all, and whether a number computed from CSS colour values can predict whether rendered text is readable.

positions.label: Ratio is the wrong math
positions.detail: sdw32 says he was surprised to find the words "contrast ratio" still in the latest WCAG 3 draft, because there is neither empirical nor theoretical evidence that the eye perceives contrast in proportion to the lightest colour divided by the darkest; the evidence supports perception of a brightness difference, which is what APCA computes. He argues that for mobile devices in typical indoor lighting the eye adapts to the room, so the difference can be used directly without normalising against an average or ambient level, and points to his cedc.tools comparison of APCA against ratio for black and white text on coloured backgrounds. Myndex adds in #29 that 4.5:1 degrades the experience for 100% of sighted users rather than only impaired ones, that roughly 86% of sites fail WCAG 2 contrast on automated survey with some of those failures being perceptual artefacts rather than real inaccessibility, and offers a side-by-side dark-mode comparison in which the WCAG 2 minimum is unreadable while the APCA minimum is legible.

positions.label: The peer review has already happened
positions.detail: Issue #29 exists to answer the Contrast Subgroup's condition that APCA needs extensive peer review before adoption. Myndex's position is that peer review is not in the WCAG 3 charter and no other subgroup has been asked for it, and that APCA has been in open public beta since the stable February 2021 release regardless. The dossier lists journal and book-published work (Ulitin in Culture and Technologies Studies 2021 and a 2023 Springer chapter), Sam Waller's Cambridge paper "Does the contrast ratio actually predict the legibility of website text?", Chris Lilley's internal W3C review in the silver repo, and a Low Vision Task Force thread involving Bailey, Campbell and Avila. He renews a 2020 proposal that AGWG convene a standing panel of subject experts on the SMPTE or ISO model, on the grounds that it would strengthen the standard's footing in future legislation.

positions.label: Testable beats theoretically correct
positions.detail: GreggVan does not dispute that stroke weight, font design, presentation time and anti-aliasing all affect reading; he says stem width was considered and dropped because most people cannot measure it, and that the current simple measure is a deliberate trade, not an oversight. What he wants from critics is proposed wording: a single statement of the musts and a second of the shoulds, where a must is important, works across web technologies and has good interrater reliability. Machine testability is not required, only enough objectivity that different evaluators reach the same conclusion. He offers to have a "text visibility" tool built that takes font, size, type, stem and height and returns a linear score against a pass threshold, with a different threshold for running text than for menus, buttons and other short strings where the reader has time to fixate.

positions.label: A test without utility is worse than no test
positions.detail: Direct rebuttal to the testability framing in #266: if the result of the test lacks utility then making it testable has not helped, and because WCAG 2.x is now being written into law, a flawed test carries flawed consequences with it. He offers the APC-RC reference-font matching method as a simple testable alternative, where a designer matches their chosen typeface against reference fonts for the silver and gold levels, necessary because "normal" and "bold" mean substantially different things per family. He also disputes GreggVan's premise that authors will not handle multiple variables, saying designers work with x-height ratio and glyph weight routinely and prefer a range of options to a binary, and that in practice only the critical content text needs testing, body text above all, and only once.

positions.label: One threshold across all weights cannot work
positions.detail: sdw32's glance-readability study, about 40 participants shown random three and four letter words for 300 ms across Open Sans Light through Extra Bold at APCA Lc 30, 45, 60 and 75, found that the minimum workable font size depends on the interaction between weight and contrast: Open Sans Extra Bold at Lc 30 outperformed Open Sans Light at Lc 75. His proposed fix is to quantify weight by pixel density, rasterising the alphabet, cropping to the x-height and thresholding at RGB(128) to split the anti-aliased pixels, after Wilkins; that gives Open Sans Light 20.2%, Open Sans 30.7%, Open Sans Semibold 40.0%, Open Sans Bold 47.5%, Open Sans Extrabold 56.4%, with Arial 35.4% and Verdana Bold 50.3%. He initially used "the quick brown fox" and then switched to the bare alphabet so the method generalises beyond Latin. TestPartners notes WCAG 2 recognises only 400 and 700 while weight 600 is common and reads as bold. patrickhlauke's objection is upstream of all of it: the same nominal CSS weight renders differently between typefaces and even between cuts of one typeface, so the value is meaningless unless anchored to specific font metrics, which font fallback then breaks.

positions.label: Nominal contrast is not rendered contrast
positions.detail: In #590 nakano0949-web proposes a rendering-aware model: a rendered glyph divides into a Core of pure glyph colour, an anti-aliased band of blended pixels, and a background ring, with Core Ratio approximated as (C/W) squared and AA Impact as 1 minus that. Measurements show AA impact climbing sharply below 14px and dominating at 12px and below, so text that passes on CSS colour values can measure substantially lower as actually drawn, worst for small sizes, thin weights and particular font cuts. He supplies a five-step extraction algorithm to automate the measurement and offers data and code. patrickhlauke cross-references the earlier w3c/wcag#4954 discussion and elsewhere in #266 lists the same class of variables the model is trying to capture: OS anti-aliasing settings, font substitution, differing cuts, and the period when macOS rendered fonts visibly fatter than Windows in the same browser.

agreed: CSS colour values alone cannot reliably predict readability. nakano0949-web's Core/AA/BG-Ring model drew no rebuttal, and Myndex confirmed the draft APC-RC already accounts for anti-aliasing.
A contrast threshold applied uniformly across all font weights is not fit for purpose. sdw32's glance data went unchallenged, including by GreggVan, who engaged with it without disputing the result.

Whatever size or contrast metric is used has to be anchored in the device-independent CSS reference px, which Myndex gives as 0.0213 degrees or 1.278 minutes of arc, rather than device pixels or any physical measurement.

Myndex's warning that WCAG 2's use of pt rather than px caused real-world error went unchallenged: designers apply the 3:1 large-text allowance at 18px when the breakpoint is 18pt, which is 24px, leaving the text 25% smaller than the standard intends.
open: Whether the minimum test stays a ratio. sdw32 asked directly in #266 and nobody from the group answered that part of his post.
Whether a rendering-aware measurement can be required of authors or is only something tools should do. nakano0949-web raised it in #590 and only patrickhlauke and Myndex replied.

Whether APC-RC serves colour vision deficient and low vision users, which nakano0949-web put to Myndex directly. Myndex answered that APCA already improves on WCAG 2 for protans, that a protan compensator extension and the SACAM adjustable colour model are in progress, and that the silver and gold contrasts target a Pelli-Robson score down to 1, but those extensions are unreleased.
GreggVan's offer to have a text visibility tool built is conditional on someone supplying the research and the interaction data to define it; no one has yet.

Whether there is any minimum requirement on the default presentation of text at all, contrast included. sdw32 argues 200% or 500% zoom is worthless if the base rendering is already inadequate; GreggVan says no. The size half of that exchange is covered under text-style-readable-minimum.
summary.note: Issue #29 is a standing evidence dossier rather than a discussion: opened in October 2023, reorganised in March 2025, last touched April 2026, and carrying no comments at all. sdw32's March 2026 objection in #266 tagged nine working group members by name (rachaelbradley, alastc, iadawn, giacomo-petri, julierawe, fstrr, MakotoUeki, hidde, GreggVan) and drew no reply in the thread; the only later comment is tsmd's note that x-height does not transfer to Japanese, Chinese or Korean.

summary.headline: Whether user-selectable font family belongs in the standard at all, and whether "accessible typeface" can ever be stated as a requirement rather than advice.

positions.label: Add font family to user customisation
positions.detail: LaZay opens #161 asking that font selection join the other user-adjustable properties in 1.4.8, noting publishers still ship serif paper fonts in digital products where they blur on screen, and that any offered families have to exist on the user's machine — a harder implementation problem than other CSS overrides. LaurenceZaysser makes the same case in #340 as a gap rather than an enhancement: 1.4.4 Resize Text has no font-family equivalent, browsers and ebook reading systems already do this, and WCAG 2.2 is therefore not the full EAA cover it is claimed to be, since Annex I requires fonts of suitable shape. Proposes a new SC 1.4.14 Change font family with a sufficient technique naming OpenDyslexic.

positions.label: Typeface guidance can be a recommendation, not a "shall"
positions.detail: Argues in #245 that a meaningful, testable normative standard covering all font use cases is out of reach, though blocks of body text might be a candidate. The reason is that line-height, letter-spacing, font-weight and font-size are all relative to decisions the font designer made, so two faces set at 16px and weight 400 rasterise at different real sizes and weights. Proposes CSS-level fixes — a property to set x-height directly, already filed with the CSSWG, and line-height expressed against x-height — and gives concrete targets: critical size is an x-height at least twice measured acuity height, lowercase aspect ratio under 1.5:1, baselines about 2.5 x-heights apart. Notes a century of research has produced little consensus beyond "blackletter is hard to read".

positions.label: Dyslexia fonts are the wrong fix
positions.detail: Directly contradicts the OpenDyslexic proposals: fonts like OpenDyslexic and Dyslexie are not actually useful, because they assume dyslexia is a visual problem when it is language-specific. Cites Marinus, Mostard et al., where increasing letter spacing on plain Arial produced the same benefit as Dyslexie, implying the gain comes from reduced crowding rather than glyph shape. Adds that dyslexia is almost unheard of in Korean, which is a clear language, so glyph-level remedies do not generalise across writing systems — of which there are at least 40 common ones.

positions.label: Untestable in practice
positions.detail: If CSS is not expressive enough for authors to declare these properties or for tools to query them from a rendered page, and font choice is effectively unlimited, a tester would have to run the numbers against every font an author picked — complicated further by user agents and operating systems shipping their own slight variants of nominally identical fonts and doing substitutions. Pushes chaals directly: if the user agent does not supply an accessible font, does the site then fail in that user agent? Draws the line at information, advice and best practice being fine, while mandatory requirements built on the same evidence is where it gets interesting.

positions.label: Put it on the user agent, and check your own fonts
positions.detail: Where the user agent supplies the font, the requirement belongs on the user agent to offer accessible fonts. Research on this has existed for a long time, so publishing information about which fonts are more accessible — and to whom, and when — should not be beyond the group. Adds the author-side corollary: if you choose fonts and want accessible content, logic says you check whether the fonts you chose achieve that.

positions.label: Extend adjustability to link decoration
positions.detail: In #413, reads G183's "if there are not a large number of links" caveat as an implicit allowance for a different treatment in high link-density content such as wikis and glossaries. Argues G182's non-underlined alternatives — blue bold, red italic — are not reliably read as links, because user expectation is anchored to underlines. Proposes a Method under the adjustable text style guideline using text-decoration-style: dotted, with a demo file attached, to keep links perceivable while cutting visual clutter.

agreed: Font metrics are not comparable across families — x-height ratio, stroke weight, kerning and leading are all designer choices with no standard, so nominal font-size and font-weight values do not describe what reaches the screen. Nobody in #245 disputed this.
Letter and line spacing have a measurable readability effect, via reduced crowding, independent of glyph design.
Publishing information and best practice about accessible typefaces is uncontroversial; only making it normative is contested.
Any typeface guidance has to be checked against non-Latin writing systems before it can be global.
open: Whether a font-family override requirement can work given the font must already be installed on the user's machine — LaZay raised the constraint and left it unresolved.
Whether WCAG 2.2 actually covers the EAA's "suitable shape" language, which LaurenceZaysser says it does not; the parallel oversight is filed against the EPUB EAA mapping as epub-specs#2752.
Where the requirement lands when the user agent supplies the font — patrickhlauke's question to chaals about whether a site fails in a user agent that offers no accessible font was never answered.
Whether OpenDyslexic should be named as a sufficient technique when Myndex's evidence says the benefit comes from spacing, not glyphs. The two threads never meet.
hata6502's dotted-underline Method, which drew no responses.
summary.note: Volume is concentrated in one place. All eight comments sit in #245, and the three other issues — #161, #340 and #413 — are unanswered bodies, so their proposals have neither support nor pushback on record. #245's own discussion is also aged: the substantive exchange is from 2022, with mraccess77 adding reading links in 2025 and no reply since.
