summary.headline: Nobody has said what the enhanced level actually raises — the two threads asking that question directly have no replies, and the shared requirements thread is arguing about whether a second, stricter threshold can be defined at all now that the baseline it would sit above has been removed.

positions.label: One scale, two cut-offs
positions.detail: Rather than write separate prose for each level, build a text visibility tool that takes font, size, type, stem and height into account and returns a linear research-based score; point it at any text and pass above X. Proposes a different X for running text, which the eye must read at speed as it passes over the line, than for menus, buttons and other short strings where the user dwells on a word. This makes enhanced a higher number on one scale instead of a second requirement, and he offers to have the tool built — but only if someone supplies the research and the interaction effects, which he asked sdw32 for directly.

positions.label: Tier by reference font, not by number
positions.detail: Because font-size and the labels normal and bold mean substantially different things across families, the APC-RC guidelines set silver and gold levels using reference fonts that a designer matches their own typeface against, a one-time exercise per font. His acuity-reserve ladder puts the enhanced step close to the minimum rather than at a doubling: 0.18 degrees, an 8.3px x-height or a 16px font at Helvetica's 0.52 ratio, is content minimum at critical size, 0.2 degrees (9.4px x-height, 18px font) is the figure for columns and blocks, and 0.24 degrees (11px x-height, 21.5px font) is preferred body. He also insists an enhanced level must not demand that everything in a view hit critical values, since spot text such as a copyright bug and sub-fluent text such as captions exist deliberately to keep the visual hierarchy readable.

positions.label: Tier by what the user cannot zoom
positions.detail: EN 301 549 already has the two-level shape this provision needs: an 8 CSS px x-height as best practice for text that can be zoomed, against a 16 CSS px x-height for text and images of text necessary for functionality that is closed to text enlargement. His glance-readability study — roughly 40 participants, random three- and four-letter words at 300 ms, across Open Sans Light through Extra Bold and APCA 30 to 75 — found Open Sans Extra Bold at APCA 30 outperforming Open Sans Light at APCA 75, so a single size threshold applied across all weights is not fit for purpose and an enhanced level would have to be a size, weight and contrast surface rather than a number. For weight he proposes Wilkins' pixel-density measure (rasterise the alphabet, crop to the x-height, threshold at RGB 128, count black pixels), giving Open Sans Light 20.2 percent, regular 30.7, semibold 40.0, bold 47.5 and extrabold 56.4 — which turns EN 301 549's body-text band of regular-to-semibold into a testable range that a stricter level could narrow.

positions.label: A narrower band has less room for rendering error
positions.detail: Every source of slop that makes the minimum hard to test bites harder on a tighter enhanced band: OS antialiasing, font fallback and substitution, different cuts of the same typeface with subtly different metrics, and browser rendering that made fonts on macOS visually fatter than on Windows. scottaohara adds that CSS scaling can change the rendered size while the specified font-size stays exactly as authored, so the declared value is not the tested value. TestPartners notes that weight 600 is very common and looks bold while strictly not being bold, so any level that keeps the binary normal/bold split has to say how intermediate values are treated. patrickhlauke supports building GreggVan's tool but treats these as the caveats it must carry.

positions.label: Replace the prohibitions with a user preference
positions.detail: The enhanced level is currently stricter by banning things — no underlining, no decorative or cursive face — and that wording is called too restrictive as a general rule and, by Myndex, subjective, ambiguous and arbitrary (the same objection recorded against the minimum). His counter-proposal reshapes what enhanced would mean: require that a plain accessible font is offered as a fallback and that layout features keep working when the user selects it, ideally through a new prefers-font-family: plain media query. The argument is that a stricter author prohibition is the wrong instrument for a dynamic medium where user personalisation can do the work, especially as these voluntary guidelines are being pressed into law.

positions.label: The stricter rule belongs at minimum
positions.detail: In #641, a voice recognition software user points out the asymmetry directly: the minimum permits some underlining and the enhanced requirement does not. Having repeatedly tried to open a link that turned out to be randomly underlined text, they want underlining restricted to links at the minimum level — which would collapse the distinction between the two levels on this point rather than preserve it. They argue underlining is a holdover from handwriting, and that digital text has bold and italic for emphasis while underlining has become the convention for links.

agreed: x-height, not CSS font-size, is the right anchor for any size threshold. sdw32 states he absolutely agrees with Myndex on this and notes deriving x-height for a given font is fairly trivial programmatically if you hold the licence; teohhanhui's observation that CSS already has the ex length unit was answered — it measures length but cannot set the rasterised size on screen — and the gap is the proposed font-x-size property (csswg-drafts #6709). Nobody argued for keeping font-size as the anchor.

Running text and short strings need different thresholds. GreggVan reaches this from testability (you dwell on a button label, you skim a line of body text) and Myndex from readability science (spot and sub-fluent text are legitimate design), and neither was contested.

A scored tool that returns one number is preferable to asking authors to look up several text characteristics and reason about how they interact. patrickhlauke endorsed the tool and only added rendering caveats.

Any absolute size in the spec should be given primarily in CSS px with pt secondary. Myndex's worked example went unrebutted: WCAG 2 specifies 18pt, designers apply the number as 18px, and the resulting text is 25 percent smaller than the standard requires.
open: What the enhanced requirement is for at all. julierawe asked in #484 whether it simply encourages developers to set default text presentation to the values already specified in the foundational adjustable text style requirement, how that connection could be made clearer, and whether that framing means customisation beyond those values is no longer encouraged. The issue has had no replies since December 2025, and she flagged the same questions against readable blocks of text enhanced (#485).

What the enhanced numbers are. The candidates on the table have never been compared: sdw32's 16 CSS px x-height for text closed to enlargement against his 8 CSS px baseline, versus Myndex's ladder from 0.18 degrees (16px font) to 0.24 degrees (21.5px font).
Whether underlining should be forbidden at enhanced only or at both levels — Finnberrys (#641), unanswered since April 2026.

Whether sdw32's pixel-density approach to font weight is sound. He asked three explicit questions — is the approach acceptable, does a free public-domain algorithm exist that could run in a website, will anyone reimplement his VBA to check his numbers — and pinged Myndex and GreggVan by name in February 2026. None has been answered.
Whether the research exists to build GreggVan's scale. He asked for the interactions; sdw32 offered his experimental data and asked to join meetings; nothing has been assembled.

Whether an enhanced tier can be specified above a floor that was removed. GreggVan confirmed there is no longer a minimum size requirement for default text presentation and sdw32 registered deep concern; the argument is recorded in full against the minimum entry, but it decides the enhanced level too, since a stricter level of nothing is still nothing.

tsmd's point that x-height does not apply to Japanese, Chinese or Korean, which every size proposal here depends on. sdw32 partly conceded the shape of the problem by replacing Wilkins' English pangram with the plain alphabet for his density metric, but that is still a Latin-script fix.
summary.note: Both issues specific to this provision — #484 and #641 — have zero comments, so everything substantive here is drawn from #266, a requirements-tracking thread shared with the minimum level and both text contrast provisions. Part of the record is also off-thread: sdw32 posted his central proposal as a .docx attachment because the GitHub editor does not support the lists and images he needed, and separately asked GreggVan for the basic process rules — whether must and should apply, whether tests have to be machine-executable, and what the deadlines are — which GreggVan answered by saying a requirement need only be objective enough that evaluators reach the same conclusion.

summary.headline: The most contested provision in the draft: what counts as readable text, how to measure it, and in which unit.

positions.label: Testability first
positions.detail: A requirement is only useful if authors can apply it and two testers reach the same verdict. CSS px is defensible as the anchor because it is defined by visual angle rather than physical pixels, so it is device-independent. Browser zoom — the default control, persistent across sites — is the user's route to larger text, so a minimum size plus available magnification is judged sufficient.

positions.label: The metric does not measure the thing
positions.detail: CSS font-size is a poor proxy for legibility: x-height and stroke weight vary enormously between typefaces at the same nominal size, and rendering differs by OS and font cut. sdw32 points to EN 301 549, which specifies x-height in CSS px (8 CSS px minimum), and proposes handling weight by pixel density rather than the binary normal/bold split. Myndex argues a test that is merely testable, without being useful, gets codified into law with unintended consequences.

positions.label: User autonomy over layout stability
positions.detail: px ignores a user's configured root font size while rem respects it, so anchoring the standard in px effectively tells the market that overriding user preference is acceptable. chaals lands in the middle: provide both a baseline that conveys a commonly legible absolute size and clear guidance that resizing must actually work — and reports from browsing ~100 pages at 64px that most sites, news sites especially, become unusable.

positions.label: Scope is too broad as written
positions.detail: "Does not use a decorative or cursive font face" is called subjective and over-broad. Finnberrys, a voice-recognition user, wants underlining restricted to links because randomly underlined text repeatedly reads as a link. julierawe wants "most text" defined before the requirement can be tested.

positions.label: Validate beyond Latin scripts
positions.detail: x-height does not translate to Japanese, Chinese or Korean, so any text-appearance metric has to be checked against non-Latin writing systems before it ships in a global standard.

agreed: WCAG 2's binary normal/bold font-weight classification is inadequate — weight 600 is common in practice and the spec must say how intermediate values are treated.
Any size metric has to be density-neutral, not "as measured on screen", because authors cannot control or test physical rendering.
The "decorative or cursive font face" wording is too restrictive to stand as a requirement.
GreggVan's framing that a requirement must be objective enough for different evaluators to reach the same conclusion, though it need not be machine-testable, went unchallenged.
open: Whether there is any minimum size requirement for default text presentation at all. sdw32 registered deep concern that it was removed; GreggVan's position is that if a size is legible for typical vision, OS magnification covers low vision.
px versus rem versus x-height as the anchoring unit.
Whether APCA replaces the 4.5:1 contrast ratio. sydneycolemanfromgoogle challenged the disruption to tooling, design systems and existing UIs and asked for research showing the benefit outweighs it.
Whether accessible typeface guidance belongs in WCAG 3 at all, given there is no CSS-queryable way to assess a font and font choice is effectively unbounded (issue #245).
summary.note: Issue #642 became contentious enough that the chair stepped in to clarify that GitHub threads are individual discussion, not a formal working-group response channel.

summary.headline: Three loosely connected threads, none of them a live argument: a long-dormant 2019-2020 debate about whether SVG text counts as an image of text, plus two unanswered proposals about where detectable text belongs and how far it goes.

positions.label: SVG text fails the intent, if not the letter
positions.detail: patrickhlauke opened #190 arguing that although SVG contains real text elements and so passes the normative definition of images of text, no user agent lets a user change the font, size or colour of that text, which is the whole point of the criterion. alastc agrees the intent is not met and proposes a split: if the text's size, position and colour must be relative to its surroundings, as in a graph or infographic, it meets the "particular visual effect" carve-out; otherwise it fails. He puts the colour half at user agents and treats the font and spacing half as inherent to SVG's purpose.

positions.label: SVG can be made to comply if authored carefully
positions.detail: Walks the criterion property by property and finds browser zoom, font size, font family, letter spacing and word spacing all work in SVG, with line-height and paragraph spacing the only genuine gaps. Argues those were not required until WCAG 2.1's 1.4.12, which only forbids preventing adaptation rather than requiring the author to offer it, so SVG text should not be held to a higher bar. Later narrows this after testing goodwitch's examples: he would only pass an SVG that inherits the document's colours, because adjusting fill values per graphic demands CSS expertise and time most users do not have.

positions.label: A sad low pass, and the group should rule
positions.detail: Built three CodePen examples and concluded that SVG with text passes, SVG with path-drawn text fails, and an svg file loaded via img fails. Pushes back on JAWS-test that High Contrast Mode is not named in the normative text and the criterion nowhere says customisation must be easy, so on a strict normative reading this has to pass. Asks AGWG to make a ruling so the industry is consistent, and suggests the real fix belongs in a WCAG 2.x release or Silver.

positions.label: Move detectable text under text-to-speech
positions.detail: Reports in #202 that the text-to-speech subgroup could find nothing specific to text-to-speech devices that a screen reader would not also cover, and proposes moving Detectable text out of Clear meaning into the Text-to-speech section to replace the Text-to-speech supported requirement. Also asks whether "text-to-speech" names the technology or the capability, suggesting a rename such as "Text as speech" if the latter, and where user-agent and TTS developer guidance would live in WCAG 3. No one has replied.

positions.label: Programmatic determinability is not enough
positions.detail: In #537, calls the provision a step in the right direction that stops short: text that is programmatically determinable but cannot be selected breaks select-to-speak. Also flags possible redundancy with the copying-supported part of "Avoid exclusionary cognitive tasks" and suggests the two may be better combined or regrouped. Unanswered.

agreed: Line-height and paragraph spacing are the properties SVG genuinely cannot expose to CSS adjustment; JAWS-test's inventory of the rest was not contested.
Text drawn as SVG paths rather than text elements fails, which nobody disputed.
open: Whether SVG text passes on a strict normative reading or fails on intent. goodwitch asked AGWG for a ruling in 2020 and none is recorded in the thread.
Whether High Contrast Mode counts as a form of setting colour and background — JAWS-test raised it and expected most of the group to say no.
shawnthompson's proposal in #202 to relocate Detectable text under Text-to-speech, and the naming question behind it.
sydneycolemanfromgoogle's point in #537 that selectability, not just programmatic determinability, is what select-to-speak needs.
summary.note: Issue #190 is a WCAG 2.x-era discussion from 2019-2020 that has drawn no comment since, now carried forward under this provision's label. The two WCAG 3-era issues, #202 and #537, are both single unanswered comments.

summary.headline: Whether fixed and sticky chrome that swallows the reflowed viewport should be a normative failure rather than an advisory technique, and in what unit such a limit could be written.

positions.label: Sticky chrome makes pages non-functional
positions.detail: WayneEDick opened #198 with screenshots of content squished between a fixed header and footer, arguing the low-resolution assumption is a phone in portrait while a low-vision user is actually in landscape, and that non-collapsible vertical panes growing with zoom leave no usable space. StommePoes says these are simply non-functional pages: at 150% on a 12-inch laptop she gets about three lines of text, and she names Medium.com and news sites as the worst offenders, failing them under text-resize in her own audits. mraccess77 adds breakages with the same cause — hover content that appears off-screen and vanishes when you scroll to it, snap scrolling that jumps past content you are trying to reach at zoom, and scroll jacking that takes away ctrl plus mouse wheel. All three treat the fix as cheap and known — WayneEDick's three techniques are switch fixed to static at low resolution, replace the bar with a control limited to 10% of the screen, or make it collapsible, and StommePoes adds that developers already write width-based media queries, so a height-based one in ems can simply drop the stickiness, since the sticky content is usually the site name or social buttons.

positions.label: A ratio threshold, worded 'down to'
positions.detail: patrickhlauke would support a percentage or ratio rule — roughly, sticky and fixed elements not covering more than a third of the visible viewport — with the understanding doc requiring testing in both portrait and landscape, down to 320 CSS px width and 256 CSS px height. He insists on "down to" rather than mandating that exact viewport dimension, because otherwise the requirement is pointless. StommePoes agrees, citing content that passed at 400% on a 1280 px viewport but broke around 250% when a media query did not fire, leaving the user to choose between 175% (too small) and 300% (larger than needed); she also reports that showing designers sticky elements eating a quarter to a half of viewport height draws no pushback, because they find it ridiculous too.

positions.label: Measurement is the blocker
positions.detail: Sticky headers create reading viewports that are too short, but mraccess77 doubts the group can reach consensus on what height is acceptable: is the metric percent of viewport height, or the number of lines of text that fit? Full coverage is clearly a failure, but two or three visible lines forcing the user to read through a slot is harder to draw a line around. He notes the LVTF concluded these issues were too challenging for WCAG 2.2's framework and belonged in Silver, and that the working group's impression is that low-vision issues are already solved — leaving him unsure which spec is the right home. alastc was more optimistic, suggesting a limit could build on reflow's existing 256 px minimum height and tie in with device orientation.

positions.label: Authors cannot be held to device density
positions.detail: PAFaieta opened #156 asking that the standard name a baseline native viewport resolution and DPI, or a baseline minimum magnification such as 200% as a satisfactory technique, on the grounds that vague language invites compliance arguments. patrickhlauke answered that CSS px is already density-independent and that authors cannot predict or test the physical resolution and dimensions users run — a person on a physically small monitor at very high resolution has chosen that, and adapting the device is their call, not the author's. alastc added that WCAG 3 deliberately avoids technology-specific language at the provision level and expects metrics to live in technology-specific methods, and asked for concrete ground-level examples of the "liberties" being taken; PAFaieta left the thread without supplying them.

positions.label: Layouts set in px are the root cause
positions.detail: chaals set font-size to 64px in Safari and browsed roughly 100 pages: news sites were generally unusable (abc.net.au the least bad), search engines were terrible, whitehouse.gov and un.org worked reasonably, and idealista was the one usable shopping site. He reports that pretty much every serious problem traced to layouts set in pixels — most commonly line-heights derived from the screen's pixel width and far below 64px, then large text squeezed into too-small boxes. His proposal is to trigger breakpoints on character counts rather than screen width in px, and to express any measure larger than half the expected font-size in rem, with layouts expected to work between 4px and 72px (about 1.5mm to 25mm). graphic-designer (#642) argues the same conclusion from user autonomy: px ignores a user's configured root font size, so a px-based architecture is rigid by construction while rem lets the layout breathe.

positions.label: Reflow itself is the barrier
positions.detail: An emailed objection alastc posted on the group’s behalf as #664 argues that forcing a 320 px mobile-style layout on a desktop display at 400% zoom increases cognitive load for older users by hiding familiar navigation and breaking established mental models. It claims this breaks complex interfaces such as legal document portals, preventing citizens from accessing documents, and characterises the mobile-first target as favouring the ecosystems of major W3C corporate members. The request is for a Desktop-Preservation Mode or a reduced requirement — 200% — that does not trigger a full layout change. Nobody has replied.

agreed: Fixed headers, footers and non-collapsible side panes that stay put under zoom render pages non-functional. StommePoes's flat "absolutely" to WayneEDick's question went unchallenged in eight years of thread.

The fixes are not technically hard — un-fixing via vertical media queries, collapsing, or allowing dismissal after reading — and no one argued they are expensive. StommePoes notes developers do not think of them but implement them readily once shown.
CSS px is density-independent, so a separate DPI or native-resolution baseline is not needed; patrickhlauke's point in #156 went unrebutted.
Technology-specific metrics belong in methods, not in provision text — alastc's framing, unchallenged.
open: Whether any limit on sticky and fixed chrome becomes normative in WCAG 3 or stays advisory as C34. alastc said in 2019 it needed volunteers; none stepped forward in the thread.
How to measure it at all — mraccess77's question of percent of viewport height versus number of readable lines remains unanswered.
What alastc's 2019 idea of building on the 256 px reflow minimum height and tying it to device orientation actually was. jake-abma asked him to lift the veil and got no reply.

Whether #198 belongs in WCAG 3 at all. scottaohara asked whether it should have been transferred rather than cloned, since his reflow understanding-doc PR would likely have addressed it in WCAG 2; cwadamsoforacle said the chairs made a blanket decision to move wcag.next issues into WCAG 3 and would review it with alastc. No further word in the thread.
Whether the 400% / 320 CSS px reflow target itself harms desktop users who do not want a mobile layout (#664), which has drawn no response.

chaals's proposed workable range of 4px to 72px is explicitly a guess; he asks for systematic research across more scripts, screen sizes, font sizes and content types, noting he covered only a handful of Chinese and Russian pages and nothing in Japanese or Arabic.
summary.note: #198 dates from 2018 (transferred from wcag21#846) and is still open with no normative outcome. #642 turned procedural: rachaelbradley intervened as chair to say GitHub discussion is between individuals, that a formal response on units may take months, and to ask for polite professionalism — after graphic-designer filed a DMCA counter-notification over his test-case file, published mirrored "audit log" copies, and reported the thread to Open Web Advocacy and Open Digital Design over other participants deleting their own comments. alastc has drafted a response closing #642 without changing any provision, but it has not been through the AG group. #664 arrived by email and has no comments at all.

summary.headline: Whether WCAG 3 should anchor sizing in CSS px or rem, and how far text-only resizing has to work.

positions.label: CSS px is already relative
positions.detail: CSS px is relative to assumed viewing distance, which is what lets a requirement say how large something must appear across platforms. alastc notes WCAG 3 does not currently use px or rem for text sizing at all, and drafted a response proposing the issue be closed without changing any provision. GreggVan adds that px has only ever been cited as a minimum, not a fixed size.

positions.label: rem respects the user, px does not
positions.detail: A user who sets a larger default font size sees rem-based layouts adapt and px-based layouts stay rigid. Argues this makes px a technical regression against user autonomy, and that calling it a user-agent problem shifts responsibility away from the standard.

positions.label: Both, and widen the resize range
positions.detail: Neither layout stability nor user scalability is the goal — people being able to read what is published is. Tested the disputed demo across Vivaldi, Avast, Safari and Firefox and found the px box adapts in some Chromium builds and not others, so the behaviour is not uniform. Proposes a separate issue: content should support text-size adjustment well beyond the current 100–200% range.

positions.label: Density is the user's call, not the author's
positions.detail: On the related question of high-DPI viewports, authors cannot predict or test the physical resolution a user runs, so a guideline cannot introduce that variability. A user running a small monitor at very high resolution has made that choice and can adapt their device.

agreed: Zoom currently works better across real sites than text-only resizing — chaals concedes this after surveying roughly 100 pages.
Requirements should avoid technology-specific language at the provision level and push metrics down into technology-specific methods.
Large headings scaling proportionally is a real layout problem, which is why the draft asks for 200% of default body size rather than 200% of starting size.
open: Whether content must support text-size adjustment beyond 200%.
Whether the spec should state a reasonable, commonly legible default text size.
Whether px-based layouts breaking under user font scaling is an author obligation or a user-agent gap.
alastc's draft response has not been through the group, so the issue is not resolved.

summary.headline: Whether an OS-level preference flag such as prefers-reduced-motion is a strong enough signal to hang a normative requirement on, or too blunt an instrument to build one from — an argument fought out in 2020 that has barely moved since.

positions.label: The preference is the requirement
positions.detail: CharlesBelov's original ask (#183) was that where the OS exposes the request and the user agent passes it to content, not animating should satisfy AA — the user telling their OS that animation is problematic removes the need for anyone to decide whether a given animation is problematic. guyhickling points out that Android's "Remove animations", iOS's "Reduce motion" and Windows 10's "Show animations" are all binary switches that set the same flag, and that honouring it costs an author a media query rather than banning animation, with an opt-in button available where the animation is genuinely informational. mgifford and guyhickling both argue AAA is where requirements go to be ignored, because AA is the procurement norm.

positions.label: A binary flag is not a mandate
positions.detail: prefers-reduced-motion is one bit, but users are affected by specific magnitudes and kinds of motion, so reading it as "no animation at all" would technically fail a page containing a single dot that fades by one opacity value. He cites Windows users who set the preference accidentally without realising what it does. His counter-proposal is the thing this provision grew out of: a generic "respect user settings" requirement at AAA covering dark mode, reduced motion and high contrast, phrased in Understanding rather than hard-coded to whichever media queries exist today, with honouring a preference offered as a sufficient technique rather than the normative bar — and even then subject to whether it is accessibility supported.

positions.label: Define the threshold and show the evidence first
positions.detail: Specifying size across devices and zoom levels, and duration when the motion is triggered by user action such as scrolling, is exactly where this stalled during WCAG 2.1. Small animations such as icons changing on hover did not appear to be vestibular triggers, so a minimum size looks necessary before the requirement can sit at A or AA. The preference is not a 1:1 fit for the user need, so relying on it produces false positives and extra work; in a consensus process that means persuading the people who objected last time. Answering CharlesBelov's invocation of the W3C Code of Conduct, he redirects to the priority-levels wiki as the document that actually governs level decisions.

positions.label: The platform plumbing does not work yet
positions.detail: JAWS-test's cross-browser test of prefers-color-scheme (#182) found Edge reporting light even in Dark Mode and dark only under high contrast white-on-black, Firefox reporting light even in HCM, Chrome mapping some HCM modes to dark and others to no-preference, Android Chrome always reporting light even in Dark Mode, and only iOS Safari behaving as expected. mraccess77 reports the Windows setting blocks animations they want along with those they do not, and asks for finer control. MarjaE2 (#40) found user CSS forcing animation-timing-function and transition-timing-function to step-start is overridden by ::before and ::after pseudo-elements carrying their own timing functions, and argues disabled users should not have to become programmers to browse without being hurt. Myndex challenges the CSS Color Adjust rule that maps Canvas lightness (L below 33% or above 67%) onto prefers-color-scheme, on the grounds that CIELAB L is not perceptually uniform on self-illuminated displays and the real flip point is higher.

positions.label: Scope the settings list, and say what respecting means
positions.detail: COGA (#737, filed by julierawe) wants haptics added to the note that currently lists font size, icon size, color scheme, magnification and motion, or the list reworded as "include but are not limited to", and asks whether the separate Haptic stimulation adjustable provision in the Animation section is still needed once haptics is covered here. JAWS-test asked the foundational question in 2020 — what does respecting a preference actually oblige an author to do, should pages invert, and what about a page already rendered light-on-dark. mgifford adds two cases nobody answered: dark mode can switch with the time of day so the preference changes mid-session without the user doing anything, and an on-page theme widget should take precedence over the browser preference.

agreed: A generic, technology-neutral "respect user settings" requirement is a better shape than per-feature criteria. patrickhlauke proposed it, mgifford agreed, and nobody argued the provision should not exist — the dispute is only over its strength and level.
Respect runs both ways: a site that is dark by default is not honouring a user who has asked for prefers-color-scheme: light. patrickhlauke's point, unrebutted.

Support for these preferences is inconsistent enough across browsers and platforms that any requirement has to be conditioned on environments that support it — JAWS-test's test results went unchallenged, with patrickhlauke cautioning only that dark mode and high contrast mode are distinct things that correlate.

Dark mode and reduced motion are not merely aesthetic preferences; mgifford's framing that people need them to read text, avoid headaches or focus went unchallenged, and patrickhlauke noted the supporting evidence is mixed and mainly concerns cloudy ocular media.
open: What "respecting" a preference concretely obliges an author to do. JAWS-test asked in 2020 and got only patrickhlauke's "take the cue from the user's preference request and actually do something about it" — no testable formulation followed.
Whether haptics belongs in the note, and whether Haptic stimulation adjustable can then be removed from the Animation section. Raised by julierawe for the COGA Task Force in #737; no replies.
Whether the note's list of accessibility-related user settings is closed or illustrative (julierawe).
How to indicate to the user when an on-site theme control diverges from their browser preference (mgifford).

Whether user-side remedies are good enough that the requirement is unnecessary. CharlesBelov's own assessment against the priority-levels wiki is that they are not: his user stylesheet sets animation-duration and transition-duration to 0 but does nothing for animated GIFs or JavaScript animation, and the only Firefox extension he found was outside Mozilla's security review.
Whether ::before and ::after overriding user CSS is a WCAG matter at all or a CSS specification defect. MarjaE2 raised it in #40 and was not sure where to report it.

Whether size and duration thresholds are the route forward (mgifford's sketch of a quantity-of-movement metric, answered by patrickhlauke's screen-rulers-and-calculators objection), or whether the preference alone suffices.
summary.note: Three of the four threads carry almost no discussion. #40 was closed without a single reply, #737 has had no response since COGA filed it in June 2026, and #182 went quiet after 2020 until one technical comment from Myndex in 2025. Effectively the whole argument lives in #183, which is dual-labelled with No visual motion and whose substance dates from 2020, with one 2025 comment from MarjaE2 reporting that drastic animation — autoplaying video, marquee text, elements that bounce or strobe once a user substitutes their own fonts — remains common, including on the W3C's own WCAG 3 introduction page.

summary.headline: A short 2020 exchange about why WCAG 2 allows autoplaying audio 3 seconds but auto-updating content 5, ending with agreement not to touch it in the 2.x series and an unpursued suggestion that WCAG 3 regroup audio with motion.

positions.label: Harmonise the limits and regroup the requirement
positions.detail: Opened #181 arguing the 3-versus-5-second split is hard to measure and has no rationale: a screen reader user is not less patient than a sighted one, and the two-second gap just adds complexity for testers. Also questions why autoplaying audio sits under Perceivable while auto-updating content sits under Operable, when unstoppable loud audio blocks operation exactly as animation does. Proposes raising 1.4.2 from 3 seconds to 5 for backwards compatibility, and treating WCAG 3 as the opportunity to group all page-level sound and animation together.

positions.label: Not worth a backwards-incompatible change
positions.detail: alastc notes the limits were set around 14 years earlier and no explanation is to hand, and that changing them would likely be backwards-incompatible — content passing WCAG 2.2 might not pass 2.0 or 2.1 — so he asks what the benefit would be. bruce-usab offers the historical guess that annoying sounds used to start immediately while animation and video took a few seconds to load, and five seconds of unwanted music was plainly too much. He does not claim the distinction is coherent, but would rather not make this change in the 2.x series.

agreed: The 3-versus-5-second difference has no principled justification anyone in the thread could produce.
Whatever the merits, it should not be changed within WCAG 2.x — bruce-usab's position, and consistent with alastc's backwards-compatibility concern.
open: Wildebrew's actual proposal — that WCAG 3 group autoplaying audio with page-level animation and auto-updating content rather than keeping them apart — was never answered and the thread stopped in April 2020.
summary.note: Three comments total, all from 2020, in a thread carrying both this provision's label and "No visual motion". Wildebrew's second comment is a mail reply with the quoted email trailer left in.
